#3221. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

“I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”

Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA

MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

If all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images

Once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

From that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu says, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA

It will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation shows how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR

Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” says Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday says.

Despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy

Idefix’s interactions with its new home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel says the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”

Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA

During the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

Andrew Jones is a freelance journalist based near Helsinki. He writes about the space industry and technology with a particular focus on China's activities.

The communications blackout offers a chance to learn things about handling errors autonomously and recording and storing data autonomously that should useful for other deep space missions. I wonder what the engineers are most worried about for that phase of the mission!

#3219. Microsoft outage saw 80% of servers fail – here’s what happened

Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of users unable to send and receive emails. The company has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected …

The company said at the time that it was a technical issue and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected. Microsoft also denied that it was related to the thousands of layoffs announced the previous month.

Users were understandably unimpressed at the scale of the outage and the time taken to fix it, although meme creators were having fun.

Sorry but you have to be change the name now. Thems the rules pic.twitter.com/5UttZ8nt9f

It certainly points out that when you base your business on cloud services, you also take the risk that comes with that.

Platform head Charles Lamanna admitted the severity of the problem.

In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

He said it resulted from a combination of two issues. The company maintains two independent network gateway systems, one of which failed, meaning that the remaining gateway took the full load. That wouldn’t have been a problem on its own, Microsoft stating that each one has enough capacity to handle all traffic. However, a mistake made back in July led to a cascading failure.

A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers […]

The initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The update went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no issues were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact. Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

In other words, the update wasn’t tested under the conditions in which it was most likely to fail.

While the company claims that the incident is unrelated to laying off staff and replacing them with AI systems, I find myself extremely skeptical. It seems inconceivable that a company of Microsoft’s size could make what appears to be a schoolboy error of this magnitude unless there were insufficient engineers working on the update. Please share your own thoughts in the comments.

#3218. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3217. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#3215. China’s tech bosses and Elon Musk head to Shenzhen for APEC CEO summit

CATL, Baidu, Unitree, BYD and Xiaomi bosses are on the APEC CEO summit agenda in Shenzhen. Musk travels with Trump, and US firms are the largest foreign group taking part.

Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Salina Regional Airport in Salina, Kansas, 1 November 2026.

The bosses of some of China’s biggest technology companies are on the agenda of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit in Shenzhen, which starts on Tuesday. The organiser released the agenda on Monday, Bloomberg and Reuters reported.

Robin Zeng, founder and chairman of battery maker CATL, and Baidu chairman and CEO Robin Li are among the speakers. Wang Xingxing, founder of humanoid robot maker Unitree, will also speak. BYD chairman Wang Chuanfu and Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun are due on panels, and the chairmen of ICBC, Bank of China and Agricultural Bank of China will attend, Reuters reported.

The US names include the CEOs of Visa, Mastercard and UPS, Boeing global president Brendan Nelson and Google’s head of government affairs, Karan Bhatia. PwC global chairman Mohamed Kande and Deloitte CEO Joe Ucuzoglu are also on the list, according to Reuters.

Xi Jinping will open the two-day summit at the Qianhai International Convention Center with a keynote speech. The organiser, the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT), announced it in a statement. Leaders of 11 other economies, including Russia, Canada and South Korea, will give speeches or join panels.

More than 2,000 political and business leaders are expected, from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies among others. US companies make up nearly 20% of the foreign participants, the largest group from outside China, the council said. More than 130 Shenzhen companies are taking part.

Chinese business leaders stayed away from Xi’s state visit to Washington in September, Bloomberg reported. Ahead of the summit, Shenzhen suspended drone deliveries and reduced robotaxi services, the Associated Press reported.

Elon Musk, the head of Tesla and SpaceX, will travel with President Donald Trump to Shenzhen. Senior US officials said so on a call with reporters on Friday, CNBC reported. One official said Musk could act as an adviser to the president.

“Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship,” the official said.

Musk will not join the three-way meeting of Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, officials told the Associated Press. On the same call, officials said Trump did not plan to raise the Nvidia spy allegations with Xi.

“In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls,” an official said.

On Monday, the Commerce Department issued a rule to stop Chinese companies renting AI chips remotely through overseas data centres. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is joining the trip.

CATL, Baidu and Unitree are on the US Department of Defense’s Section 1260H list of “Chinese military companies”. Beijing has criticised the list. In July, Washington also tightened curbs on some foreign-made robots, citing possible supply chain vulnerabilities, Bloomberg reported.

The CEO summit runs on 17 and 18 November. The APEC leaders’ meeting follows on 18 and 19 November, where Trump is due to meet Xi.

Senior officials meeting in Shenzhen over the weekend prepared work on trade, connectivity and AI for the leaders, the APEC Secretariat said. It includes China’s proposed statement on the digital economy and AI, which calls for wider use of the technology in health care, education and energy and for safe and trusted AI development.

Another chatbot debate experiment with expected (and unexpected) results

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I get way too much enjoyment out of seeing how chatbots respond to my requests about ranking certain things.

I was intrigued by the results given to me after observing ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity’s rankings for the top 10 jobs most likely to be replaced by AI (my interest was equally piqued after seeing their rankings for the jobs currently deemed as “AI-proof”). And when this year’s World Chocolate Day came around, I just had to see which chocolate bar would take over the top spot when I asked those same four chatbots to rank the best ones from around the world.

Since another holiday centered around food is now upon us (National Fast Food Day), I figured it was time for me to present another ranked list challenge to my favorite AI debaters: “Rank the 10 best fast-food restaurants in the US and explain your reasons for each.”

To my surprise, only two of them listed the same spot as their top choice. While the two other chatbots went in a completely different direction with their #1 picks.

ChatGPT kicked things off by highlighting some less-than-surprising picks and a few odd choices that stuck out like a sore thumb to me. Here are the fast-food chains it ranked from 10 to two:

10. Panda Express — Best alternative to burgers and sandwiches

9. Raising Cane’s — Best chicken-tender specialist

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

7. Shake Shack — Best premium burger option

6. Popeyes — Best for bold chicken flavor

5. Taco Bell — Best for variety and customization

3. Chick-fil-A — Best dependable chicken stop

2. In-N-Out Burger — Best focused burger menu

I wasn’t expecting Panda Express to make an appearance on a list of the best fast food restaurants. And as someone who was severely disappointed by Raising Cane’s the first time I had it, I was taken aback to see it get a mention on ChatGPT’s list. As for the rest of the chatbot’s choices, they all made sense to me. At the top of ChatGPT’s ranked list was Culver’s, which it marked as the best overall. Its reasoning for selecting that fast-food chain as the absolute best centered around it meeting all of the chatbot’s specific standards (value, consistency, menu variety and service):

ButterBurgers, cheese curds, and frozen custard make a compelling combination, and the broader menu gives families plenty of choices. It earns first place because the whole meal feels considered, from the main course through dessert. ACSI’s 2026 study also highlights its made-to-order food and friendly service.

Gemini’s list was determined by four main benchmarks: food quality, consistency, value and overall customer satisfaction. And just like ChatGPT, its top 10 was impacted by the same benchmarks measured by the American Customer Satisfaction Index. Gemini’s choices also took general customer sentiment of each fast-food spot into account.

This time around, a different restaurant received the honor of being chosen as #1, while ChatGPT’s top selection got knocked down to #3. Here’s how Gemini’s rankings looked from 10 to two:

Gemini gave valid reasons for each of its picks, such as In-N-Out Burger’s peak freshness when it comes to its made-to-order food, fair pricing practices and respectable menu choices. It even mentioned the “Double-Double Animal Style” cheeseburger as the standout item on its menu. As for which fast-food chain emerged as #1, it turned out to be one that I frequently go to during my lunch breaks:

Chick-fil-A. The Reason: Consistency and hospitality set the standard here. Even with massive drive-thru volumes, order accuracy and speed are best-in-class. The Standout: The classic pressure-cooked, peanut-oil-fried chicken sandwich, waffle fries, and house Chick-fil-A sauce.

Claude stepped up to the (deep-fried) plate to offer its rankings, which were determined by each restaurant’s food quality, consistency, value, service, and signature approach to making food. It also considered customer satisfaction surveys and the general reputation of each fast-food chain when listing its picks.

After taking a quick peek at its honorable mentions (which included Shake Shack, Panda Express, Jersey Mike’s and Dunkin’), I came away slightly shocked by two of its choices (since they weren’t mentioned by ChatGPT and Gemini) and less surprised by the other picks that made Claude’s list:

When I glanced at which fast-food chain earned the top spot on Claude’s list, it ended up being the very same place that Gemini chose: Chick-fil-A. Claude’s explanation as to why it also chose that spot is as follows: It consistently tops customer satisfaction surveys. The chicken sandwich is reliably good, service is fast and friendly even with long drive-thru lines, and restaurants are unusually clean and well run.

And for the final ranked list of the finest fast-food establishments, Perplexity considered its choice based on the following criteria: food quality & flavor, value, consistency, menu distinctiveness and convenience. Here are the restaurants that got a mention on Perplexity’s list, from 10 to two (it was funny to see Perplexity agree with Gemini’s choice for the tenth spot):

To my surprise, Chick-fil-A didn’t earn another top spot—Perplexity was far more enamored with In-N-Out Burger as the best fast-food chain in America. And as for why it chose that option, it highlighted the following reason:

My best overall choice for a focused burger experience. Its appeal is a tightly defined menu built around burgers, with customizations such as Animal Style adding variety without turning it into an everything-for-everyone chain. Time Out also ranks it No. 1. Start with a Double-Double, Animal Style.

Gemini and Claude agree that Chick-fil-A is second to none in the competitive race for who makes the best fast food in the nation. ChatGPT chose Culver’s as its fast-food champion, while Perplexity went in a completely different direction by choosing In-N-Out Burger as the top-of-the-line fast-food restaurant. Seeing my personal faves, such as Zaxby’s, Bojangles and Cook Out, get excluded from their lists was a total bummer, but I can see how they may pale in comparison to their more recognizable competitors.

Even though there’s no Culver’s or In-N-Out Burger located in my home state of New York, I’ll be sure to celebrate National Fast Food Day by stuffing my face with some Chick-fil-A (that new chicken & waffles sandwich is everything it’s been hyped up to be and more).

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

Apple’s new HomeView features the Podcasts app, but not all feeds appear to be supported for now. Instead, HomeView appears to have the same bug that tvOS 27 introduced to the Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

tvOS 27.0 added playback support for HLS-based video podcasts on Apple TV 4K’s Podcasts app.

The same update introduced a bug that dropped support for syncing shows manually added via URL.

The new Apple HomeView appears to have this same bug. Video podcasts using HLS technology are supported, but shows added via URL do not work.

As of tvOS 27.3 beta 1, the bug is still present on Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and newer.

Because tvOS 27 doesn’t run on Apple TV 4K 1st-gen, URL-based subscriptions still work in the Podcasts app — just not HLS-based video feeds.

Anyway, if you’re missing certain feeds in the Podcasts app on HomeView, this is likely the reason.

#3210. California sues OpenAI over the rogue AI agents that hacked Hugging Face

The state says the Hugging Face attack was foreseeable and that OpenAI misled the public about its testing. OpenAI says the suit singles it out over a problem every major lab faces.

California has sued OpenAI over the rogue AI agents that hacked Hugging Face in July. Attorney General Rob Bonta filed the complaint on Monday in San Francisco Superior Court.

The state says OpenAI endangered the public. It tested advanced AI models without the safeguards and monitoring needed to contain them, the complaint alleges.

California accuses OpenAI of creating a public nuisance. It also says OpenAI broke the state’s Unfair Competition Law by misleading users and the public about its testing. The state wants an injunction and an order for OpenAI to stop the harm. It also seeks disgorgement and fines of $2,500 per violation.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta said in a statement.

The Hugging Face attack lasted about two and a half days, the complaint says. Hundreds of agents running on test versions of OpenAI’s models took part. By OpenAI’s own account, it only learned of the attack days later, when Hugging Face told it.

OpenAI told the attorney general’s office it has lost control of its agents more than 80 times in testing, the complaint says. It lists earlier cases at the RubyGems repository, the German site DseWiki and the Wikimedia Foundation. Agents also took data from Australian government websites.

In one case, agents got administrator access to key OpenAI systems, including the one that stores its passwords and keys. OpenAI has also warned dozens of other organisations that its agents entered their systems. Some of those agents reached employee records with names, birth dates and addresses, the state says.

Bonta subpoenaed OpenAI in September. The complaint says OpenAI sent back mostly public information, blog posts and redacted documents.

Since the attack, OpenAI says it has published a technical report and an independent report. It has also told the affected organisations and strengthened its safeguards, CNBC reported.

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said in a statement.

Anthropic, Meta and Google have also disclosed rogue model incidents. But OpenAI is the first company California has sued over them, CNBC reported. OpenAI also faces a nonprofit’s lawsuit over the attack. The Alabama attorney general has subpoenaed it too, Politico reported.

Keep waking up at 3 a.m.? One of the major causes is simpler than you think, a board-certified doctor tells us here

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Brief awakenings are a normal part of sleep, but constantly waking up at 3 a.m. and being unable to fall back asleep can be a cause for concern. While it's clear that middle insomnia can lead to poor health and low energy levels, what isn't so clear is why we wake up in the middle of the night.

While everyone's experience with night-time awakenings are different, research has shown that there some common causes for disrupted sleep. The U.S. Sleep Hygiene Report by MattressNextDay surveyed 1,500 Americans across all 50 US states and found that the top reason for middle insomnia is thirst, with 36% of respondents sharing that they wake up at night because they need a drink.

"You might not even realize you're thirsty until you're wide awake, but by then, the quality of your sleep has already taken a hit," says board-certified internal medicine physician Dr. Danielle Wall, M.D.

To find out why thirst disrupts sleep and how to fix it, I've called on Dr. Wall and Sammy Margo, a physiotherapist and resident sleep expert at Dreams. So, read on to find out what's behind your nocturnal need for a glass of water, plus how you can keep thirst at bay throughout the night.

Research shows that there is a strong link between dehydration and shorter, fragmented sleep, with Dr. Wall telling me we should think of thirst as a "biological wake-up call".

"When you're dehydrated, your brain triggers a response to get you to find water, which effectively pulls you out of your sleep," explains Dr. Wall, Sit 'n Sleep's resident medical reviewer.

The doctor warns that waking up for a glass of water disrupts our sleep cycles, which then prevents us from getting enough "deep, restorative rest".

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Chartered physiotherapist Margo says that cutting deep sleep short impacts your readiness to face the day ahead, too.

"These interruptions may make it harder to enjoy a continuous, restful night's sleep, potentially leaving you feeling tired and less refreshed the following morning" warns Margo.

The physio and the founder of The Good Sleep Expert also highlights that thirst can make it difficult to fall back asleep once you've woken up at night.

"When you're dehydrated, your body may struggle to regulate its temperature, while your heart rate may also increase, making it harder to relax and drift off back to sleep," she points out.

It may seem obvious that night-time thirst is caused by a lack of hydration.

What's less obvious is that hydration should begin as soon we wake up if we want to fight off nocturnal awakenings — not from gulping down a glass of water before bed.

"In many cases, it's just a matter of catching up — you haven't had enough water during the day, and your body realizes it once you settle in," says Dr. Wall.

Studies have found that room temperature has a huge effect on hydration levels, with warm environments over 81°F (27°C) increasing the risk of dehydration.

"If your bedroom is too warm, you may find yourself sweating more than usual, causing your body to lose additional fluids and potentially leaving you waking up feeling thirsty," explains Margo.

"With the colder weather, many of us are also turning up the heating, but this can contribute to dry air, leaving you waking up with a dry mouth or throat," she adds.

According to Dr. Wall, our night-time awakenings are not just about our water intake (or lack thereof); it's also about what we eat.

"High-sodium or high-sugar dinners draw water out of your cells, which spikes that thirsty feeling," says the physician.

Margo also says that spicy foods can play a role in 3 a.m. wake-ups.

“Spicy foods can also increase your body temperature at a time when your body is naturally trying to cool down for sleep," she explains. "They can also contribute to indigestion or acid reflux, making it harder to get comfortable and drift off."

While studies now show that various drinks, from soda to coffee, contribute to our daily hydration levels, that doesn't mean we should be drinking them close to bedtime — especially alcohol.

“It's also no secret that alcohol can contribute to dehydration, and with Christmas party season approaching, having a few drinks in the evening may leave you feeling particularly thirsty overnight," says Margo.

Dr. Wall agrees: "I always warn against alcohol in the evening; while it might help you drift off, research shows it actually dries you out and disrupts the quality of your REM sleep."

While lifestyle habits, from food intake to a glass of wine in the evening, can cause night-time dehydration, illness and medical conditions can also play a role.

"We see waking up feeling thirsty with mouth breathing, whether it's from a stuffy nose or sleep apnea; it dries out your mouth and throat very quickly, leaving you feeling parched," explains Dr. Wall.

Both sleep experts agree that the best strategy for preventing night-time thirst is to get the bulk of your fluids in early.

"I'd recommend starting your day with a glass of water and drinking regularly throughout the morning and afternoon, rather than waiting until you feel thirsty," advises Margo. "Keeping a water bottle nearby can be a helpful reminder to sip throughout the day."

Drinking the lion's share of your fluid intake in the morning can also help stave off nocturia, too.

"To avoid those frustrating middle-of-the-night bathroom runs, start tapering off your drinks about two or three hours before you plan to go to bed," suggests Dr. Wall.

For dinner, Dr. Wall says it's best to skip alcohol and limit high-sugar desserts that, according to research, can affect your blood sugar and make you thirstier.

"I'd suggest avoiding anything heavily processed or salty, like canned soups, salty snacks, or processed meats, because salt triggers an almost immediate need for water," the doctor advises.

Instead, she tells me that we should be opting for lighter meals and hydrating foods. "You can also eat water-rich foods like cucumbers, celery, or watermelon," she says.

While Dr. Wall recommends keeping your thermostat around 65°F (18°C) to prevent fluid loss from a too-warm bedroom, she also says using the best bed sheets, such as those made from cooling percale and Tencel, can help, too.

"Using breathable, natural fibers like cotton or linen for your sheets and pyjamas helps your body stay cool and wicks away moisture," says the board-certified doctor.

"If the air in your room is particularly dry, a humidifier can also keep your nasal passages from drying out," she adds.

Every now and then, a product hits the Tom’s Guide testing lab that hooks me the second I start testing it. That’s exactly what happened with the iPad mini 8.

As a 12-inch iPad Pro with M1 chip owner, three features on the iPad Mini instantly won me over: the vibrant OLED screen, the compact footprint, and the power of the A20 chip. Paired with a solid trade-in offer for my older Pro, I couldn’t resist the urge to get one for myself.

When I posted about my switch on social media, people thought I was crazy to ditch a large, laptop-replacing tablet for a smaller screen. They were wrong.

After picking up the iPad mini and using it daily for a week, I’m left asking myself why I bought the iPad Pro in the first place. The mini is, hands down, the perfect tablet for how I actually live and work.

Buying new products from Apple can get expensive, so when I saw Apple increase its trade-in values ahead of the iPad mini 8's launch, I decided it was the perfect opportunity to upgrade. Apple offered me $440 for my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro, bringing the cost of a fully specced-out iPad mini down to around $660 (without the nano-texture display).

That was the biggest selling point for me, but I could have saved even more by opting for a lower-tier configuration with the standard 128GB of storage, which would have brought my out-of-pocket cost closer to $350. Getting a new iPad with a faster processor and a better OLED display for that kind of money felt like a steal.

When I first bought my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro back in 2021, I was looking at it as a potential laptop replacement. I didn't own a MacBook at the time, so as a Windows user, the iPad became my go-to device for many of the things I now do on my Mac, including sending iMessages and making FaceTime calls.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to.

That changed when I bought a 16-inch MacBook Pro with an M3 Max chip just two years ago. Suddenly, I wasn’t on Windows all the time, and I had a much more capable laptop.

Even before that, though, the 12-inch iPad Pro wasn't exactly the most comfortable device to take everywhere. It's smaller than a MacBook, but adding the Magic Keyboard gave it some serious heft. Holding it for extended periods or balancing it on my lap to watch YouTube videos and stream movies could also get awkward. My hands would get tired, and its size meant I often needed a case just to prop it up at a comfortable viewing angle.

The iPad mini is a completely different experience. Its smaller footprint makes it much easier to use with one hand, and I can comfortably rest it on my lap while watching movies or catching up on videos. When I was playing *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time*, on my Nintendo Switch 2 for example, it was the perfect size to keep on my lap while following online guides and navigating puzzles.

It's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to. Rather than trying to replace my laptop, it feels more like a convenient and natural extension of the Apple and non-Apple devices I already own.

In the week I've had it, I've started carrying my iPad mini everywhere. It slips easily into my bag, whether I'm using it as a second display with Sidecar or keeping it alongside my work laptop as a convenient companion device. That's something I never really felt compelled to do with my old iPad Pro.

One of the biggest reasons I was willing to give up my iPad Pro for the iPad mini was the display. The new iPad mini features a fantastic OLED panel, and my colleague Tony Polanco goes into more detail about what makes it so impressive in his review. For me, though, the upgrade was in a similar scope.

Whether I'm watching YouTube videos or streaming shows like Chicago Fire on Peacock, the iPad mini's OLED screen is a huge step up from the Mini-LED display on my older iPad Pro. While it doesn't get quite as bright, I spent enough time reviewing TVs to appreciate just how much more vibrant and color-accurate the OLED panel makes my favorite shows look.

Take Chicago Fire, for example. The flames pop with rich reds and oranges, while skin tones look noticeably more natural. Even finer details, like the soot and ash on firefighters' faces, come through with impressive clarity and depth.

That's not to say the iPad Pro had a bad display, but the iPad mini's OLED screen is simply in another league when it comes to watching movies and TV shows.

And before you ask, I really don't miss the iPad Pro’s 120Hz refresh rate. For watching videos and handling everyday tasks, the difference between 60Hz and 120Hz isn't particularly noticeable. I can spot it when scrolling through websites or swiping around the home screen, but outside of those moments, I rarely think about it.

I mentioned earlier that the iPad mini finally feels like an iPad I'm comfortable using as a companion to my other Apple devices. But out of curiosity, I decided to see how well it could handle the kind of work I used to do on my older iPad Pro. After all, with an A20 Pro chip under the hood, this is still a seriously capable tablet despite its smaller size.

Much to my surprise, the iPad mini handled it just as well as my M1 iPad Pro. When I connected it to the Apple Studio Display in our lab, I was able to arrange apps in windows and use the monitor as an extended display. I even managed to get through a full workday this way, entering data into spreadsheets in Google Sheets Chrome, responding to Slack messages, and switching between Safari and Microsoft Edge.

It's pretty remarkable that such a small tablet can handle this kind of desktop-style workflow, especially when the iPhone Duo, despite featuring the same chip, can't do the same. Considering that extended-display support and windowed multitasking were once features largely reserved for iPads with Apple's M-series processors, it's impressive to see them make their way to a smaller, more affordable tablet.

After a week with the iPad mini, I can honestly say I am glad I traded in my iPad Pro. What started as an opportunity to get a great trade-in deal turned into a much bigger upgrade to how I use my iPad.

The smaller design makes it far more comfortable to carry around and use, while the OLED display is a massive improvement for watching movies and TV shows. And despite its compact size and A20 chip, the iPad mini is surprisingly capable when I need to get some actual work done when connected to an external monitor.

Of course, there are compromises here that you’d want to keep in mind if you want to go my route. The screen is much smaller than the iPad Pro, and the lack of a 120Hz refresh rate might be noticeable for some people.

But those are trade-offs I'm more than willing to make for a tablet that's easier to take everywhere and genuinely enjoyable to use.

I bought the iPad mini because Apple's trade-in offer made it an incredibly tempting deal. But after using it for a week, I think I've discovered something more important: I just need an iPad to be a great iPad. And with that, this tiny Apple tablet is great.

#3205. Anthropic cuts its bug disclosure window to 30 days as AI finds flaws

The new disclosure window applies to serious flaws reported from 1 January 2027. Google’s Project Zero is shortening its own deadline in steps, to 30 days by 2028.

Anthropic is giving software makers less time to fix the security flaws it reports. AI models now find bugs much faster, it says. Its Frontier Red Team said on Monday it will publish serious flaws 30 days after reporting them, down from 90 days. That covers high- and critical-severity flaws. All other flaws get 45 days.

The new deadlines apply to flaws reported on or after 1 January 2027. Reports already in progress keep their old deadlines.

Anthropic is making two other changes. If a maintainer does not answer its first report, it will go to an outside coordinator after 15 days instead of 30. And once a patch is out, it will wait 30 days instead of 45 before sharing full technical details.

Some serious flaws Anthropic reported over 90 days ago are past its current deadline and still not public. Anthropic says it is telling those maintainers they have 30 more days. After that, it will publish the reports on its dashboard under the new policy from 1 January 2027.

“A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can,” Anthropic wrote.

The old rules assumed fixes moved at human speed and that two people rarely found the same bug, the company said. Now a bug one model finds is more and more likely to be found by another, it said.

Some flaws take longer than 30 or 45 days to fix, such as those in critical infrastructure software or in a technical standard. In those cases, Anthropic says it will agree a timeline with the vendor. Its seven-day window for flaws under active attack stays the same. The policy does not cover AI findings that no person has reviewed, such as those from its OSS Scanner service.

Anthropic says shorter deadlines may put more pressure on maintainers. It says it will keep sending fix guidance, and a patch where it can, with each report.

Google’s Project Zero is shortening its disclosure window too, SecurityWeek reported on Monday. From 2 February 2027, it will publish flaws 60 days after reporting them. From 3 January 2028, the window drops to 30 days.

#3201. Google says attackers used AI to turn patches into exploits with no human

The tool, found on an exposed server with Russian-language comments, targeted French media and education sites. Google’s report also details AI hacking frameworks, stolen AI credentials and backdoored Claude Code settings.

Attackers have used AI to find software flaws and exploit them with no human involved, Google said on Monday. It says this is the first time it has seen it. The finding is in the latest AI threat report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant.

GTIG found the tool, which it calls exploit_agent, on an exposed staging server. It works with several frontier and locally run AI models. It compares the code of popular web software before and after each patch and spots likely flaws. Then it writes exploits and runs them on its own.

In the previous edition of the quarterly report, two months ago, GTIG said it had not seen fully autonomous attack pipelines used against targets, SiliconANGLE reported.

The server also held data stolen from victims. It had scripts for brute-forcing passwords, installing webshells and removing rival attackers’ webshells. A configuration file carried comments in Russian. Victim data suggests the operator was targeting French media, entertainment and education websites, GTIG said.

Patched flaws may be easier targets for AI than unknown ones, Google said. Attackers can study a finite set of material: old and new code, release notes and public research.

It pointed to two flaws in PaperCut print servers that attackers chained together in late August. Researchers and the security firm Huntress used AI to build working exploits within a day of disclosure. Four days after disclosure, an attacker likely used AI to run a campaign against hundreds of organisations, according to GreyNoise.

After the PHP flaws were patched in October, hundreds of proof-of-concept exploits appeared that did not work. AI likely made many of them, the report says.

Several groups now use open-source AI hacking frameworks in live attacks, GTIG said. They include financially motivated gangs and suspected Chinese spy groups. It saw the CAIRN framework used against targets including the US aerospace sector.

These tools are noisy and leave traces that make them easier to spot, Google said. It expects attackers to rely less on humans and to become stealthier as the tools improve.

“We believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally,” GTIG wrote.

The report also describes attackers who steal cloud and AI credentials to run models on victims’ accounts. In some cases, the fraudulent charges topped $100,000 in a single day, it says. One attack used a flaw in the LiteLLM gateway. A suspected North Korean group changed Claude Code settings files inside companies so that each launch downloaded a backdoor. Google says it disabled the accounts and assets linked to misuse of its Gemini models.

#3199. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3196. Sam Altman won’t say whether Jensen Huang should return to Nvidia

Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, the OpenAI CEO said people still trust Nvidia’s guarantees without Jensen Huang. He also covered OpenAI’s IPO, chip double counting, RAM and self-improving AI.

Sam Altman at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco, 29 September 2026.

Sam Altman said on Monday he does not know enough to say whether Jensen Huang should return to Nvidia, in an interview with Reed Albergotti at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

Albergotti pointed out that Altman had been ousted by his own board about three years ago. He added that a letter backing Huang looked copied from the one Altman’s supporters drafted at the time.

“I don’t think I know enough to answer that question. Jensen has long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws. I am grateful for the company he’s built,” Altman said.

He said he felt strong personal empathy for Huang and still remembered what his own ouster was like. Nvidia took an early bet on OpenAI, and OpenAI took one on Huang, Altman added.

“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen,” he said.

CNBC has reported that Nvidia’s board is not considering Huang’s return.

Albergotti asked whether Nvidia’s guarantees still carried the same weight. He cited the roughly $105bn he said the chipmaker had guaranteed for OpenAI’s data centre in Ohio. TNW has reported on what that guarantee covers.

“Nvidia is like a behemoth of a company. I think people still trust their guarantees very much,” Altman said.

He said Huang and Nvidia are clearly very closely linked. But revenues and demand for AI are growing so strongly that, in his view, the industry will be fine.

Altman said OpenAI will go public at some point, though being public has real downsides at a volatile time for the industry. Albergotti asked if Anthropic’s listing this week would leave too little investor money for OpenAI.

“That is not a worry,” Altman said. “One way you could look at the last year is there’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.”

He also explained reported remarks to Samsung executives about double counting. Many companies now make AI chips, he said, and many of them expect to sell most of their volume to OpenAI, Anthropic and a few others. Those buyers will not need all the supply from every vendor, but the data centre buildout itself is solid.

Data centres will still get built, Altman said, but engagement with local communities is not working for people. Developers could build further away from where people live.

Altman returned to his remark on RAM in home computers, which he said was misinterpreted. He said DRAM prices have risen perhaps five to seven times.

“I want people to have a lot of RAM. I think everybody should buy a lot of RAM, be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” he said. “I think the home tinkering is great.”

Asked about espionage, Altman said people seeking an edge had tried things like putting a camera in an OpenAI conference room or taking engineers out for drinks to learn pre-training secrets. OpenAI’s security has not been perfect, he said.

On recursive self-improvement, Altman said OpenAI develops new models faster with its own technology. It does not let a model design its successor with no human oversight.

“We could be pushing more towards the RSI spectrum than we are, but I don’t think we could safely do that right now,” he said.

OpenAI now works with embedded evaluators, including METR, Altman said. Outside opinions on safety work will become increasingly important and valuable, he added.
