#3195. Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

The usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ plan. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

Anyone still waiting on an iPhone Duo pre-order from the Apple Store may want to check their delivery dates. Because your foldable might be arriving a little earlier than Apple originally promised. That's what various users on the MacRumors forums have been saying, anyway.

The most excitable of users have posted about how their initial arrival estimate was in late January, but over the last few days it seems to have changed to mid-to-late December instead. One user noted that they ordered two Duos on pre-order day, five minutes apart. The first arrived on launch day (October 23), while the other had a January 25 delivery estimate — which has just changed to the same mid-December window.

Some users even posted screenshots of their delivery estimate moving to mid November — which is right around now.

Obviously, the question of why Apple has suddenly changed these delivery estimates is being discussed at great length. Some speculate that this could be down to Apple narrowing down when it can actually deliver iPhone Duos, since pre-order delivery estimates defaulted to January extremely quickly.

Others speculate that it could be the fact that more people have been cancelling pre-orders for some reason or another. There are reasons why that might be the case, such as picking the phone up from a third party retailer able to deliver sooner than Apple.

Alternatively, others may have decided the iPhone Duo isn't for them. Whether that's down to the cost, the lengthy wait times, or the issues with broken screens, is unclear. However, canceled pre-orders mean that other people move up the line and get their units faster. Similarly any Duos that are returned unopened, possibly failed scalpers or anyone with buyer's remorse, will likely be put back into circulation.

Anyone ordering an iPhone Duo from Apple right now will still be stuck with a January 22 delivery date. Still, with the new year coming up fast, it's not as bad a prospect as it was back when pre-orders opened.

#3193. macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

#3192. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3191. Ramaphosa says Musk’s ‘difficulty’ with policy keeps Starlink out

Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley event, South Africa’s president said Musk does not understand what apartheid did. Starlink remains unlicensed while a court bid challenges the 30% ownership rule.

Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa, at the COP28 climate summit in Dubai, 2 December 2023.

Elon Musk’s difficulty with South Africa’s ownership policy is what keeps Starlink out of the country, President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Monday. He was speaking to ABC News’ Jonathan Karl at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event in California.

South Africa’s telecoms law sets at least 30% ownership by historically disadvantaged groups for individual licences, TechCentral reported. SpaceX has refused to give up 30% of its local operation, so Starlink’s entry has stalled.

Communications minister Solly Malatsi told Icasa in December 2025 to consider equity-equivalent investment programmes instead. In May 2026, Icasa said it could not fully apply that direction without a change to the law. On 9 November, business group Sakeliga asked the Pretoria high court to set Icasa’s decision aside, according to TechCentral.

Musk grew up in South Africa. He has called its rules “openly racist ownership laws”, in a February 2025 post on X. Karl said Musk has also accused Ramaphosa of building an apartheid 2.0.

Ramaphosa said Musk is conservative by nature and does not fully understand what apartheid did to Black South Africans. The apartheid government spent 12 rand on Musk’s education for every one rand it spent on his, Ramaphosa said.

“If one does not understand that, one will never be able to understand precisely what needs to be done to remedy the harm that was done,” he said.

Ramaphosa said there had been talk of a meeting with Musk on this trip, but their diaries had not matched. He said Musk’s brilliance had awed him in the past.

“Even as one is a citizen of a new country, you should still be loyal to your old country,” Ramaphosa said.

Musk owes what he has become to his education in South Africa, Ramaphosa added. He should give back to the country, he said. Karl also noted that Musk had been involved in the US midterms, where his candidates lost almost everywhere.

Ramaphosa called his Oval Office meeting with Donald Trump an ambush. Trump showed him videos there that he said were from South Africa. He said Trump was seriously misinformed, because the video and press clippings did not show South Africa.

“We are Nelson Mandela’s children and we respect the human rights of everyone. Black, white, everyone,” he said, adding that there is no white genocide in South Africa.

He said falsehoods have shaped how the US relates to South Africa. He and Trump have not spoken since that meeting.

US voters have pushed back against AI data centres, and ballot measures rejected them. South Africa has had the opposite experience, Ramaphosa said. The country is home to almost 70% of the data centres built on the African continent, he said.

His biggest worry about AI is technology out of human control, he said. He raised the point at the BRICS meeting in India. He said he agreed with AI leaders who call for global guardrails, and warned against autonomous weapons making decisions.

Ramaphosa said he would hold meetings with OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, and with their investors. His delegation of nearly 300 people includes ministers, South African tech firms, and students. He wants more US companies to join the 600 already operating in South Africa.

#3190. iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

#3187. Chase blames a software bug for online banking problems at US banks

JPMorgan Chase said the software bug sat in its own on-premise hardware and hit other banks only through transactions with Chase. Thousands reported problems, days after outages at Microsoft and the FAA.

JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug in its own on-premise hardware for Monday’s online banking problems at several big US banks. The bank said in a post on X that there was no evidence of a cyberattack. It aims to fix the issue by the end of the day.

JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.

Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue.

Customers still have access to their accounts and funds.

We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today.

Other banks felt it only where they were party to a transaction with Chase, the bank said, and “this is not a systemic issue.” Its customers still have access to their accounts and funds.

Reports about Chase on Downdetector peaked at nearly 5,000 around 2pm ET, Forbes reported. Customers of Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle also logged problems, in smaller numbers.

Of the Chase reports, 52% concerned balances and transactions, 21% web log-ins and 17% transfers, The Hill found. Chase’s app told customers that some services were not available.

Some Chase customers said on social media they could not use ATM cards or finish transactions in branches. The New York Times reported those posts.

The problems centred on Chase customers and on people at other banks trying to transact with Chase, the Associated Press reported. Bank of America and Citigroup had no problems with their own services, according to the AP.

“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank said in a statement.

Zelle, which a group of banks owns through Early Warning Services, said its network was working.

“An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” a Zelle spokesperson said.

The Federal Reserve’s own payment systems, including ACH transfers between banks, kept working normally. ABC News reported that from the Fed’s website.

The banking problems followed Microsoft’s Outlook outage, which began on Thursday. Microsoft called that a technical issue, unrelated to cyberattacks or AI agents.

On Friday, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after its air traffic communications network failed. Officials traced it to an Arkansas router upgrade. The FAA said it was not a cybersecurity incident either.

There was no indication the bank problems were related to Microsoft’s outage, The New York Times reported.

#3186. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3185. iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates

iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.

When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.

Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’

You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

What do you think of Apple Calendar’s design updates in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

#3183. Satya Nadella says Claude Code caught Microsoft off guard and the IDE faded

On The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Satya Nadella said Microsoft had no quick answer when coding moved to the command line. He also explained the voluntary exit offers and the slowdown in junior hiring.

Microsoft chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on stage at Microsoft Build 2026 in San Francisco

Anthropic’s Claude Code caught Microsoft off guard by moving coding from the editor to the command line, Satya Nadella said. Within about six months, the IDE “kind of faded away,” he told Gergely Orosz on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast.

Orosz, a former Microsoft engineer, recorded the hour-long interview in Redmond. It took place a few hours before Microsoft’s Outlook outage last Thursday, so the outage did not come up. Nadella also talked about Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers, junior hiring, and checking AI-written code.

Orosz asked how Microsoft, with GitHub Copilot and VS Code, had no immediate answer when Claude Code arrived in 2025. Nadella said Copilot began as code completion, and that Cursor then built a strong agent mode, which Microsoft matched.

“The thing that hit us was obviously the great work that Anthropic did with their model, which then truly made the CLI the form factor,” Nadella said.

“When model jumps happen nonlinearly, the form factor has to change quickly. AI-first product building in that sense is unforgiving,” he said. “Don’t be in love with what you built.”

He said the IDE could come back as developers embed decision models inside software. He called those models the stored procedures of the intelligence era.

Orosz asked directly whether Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers were a prelude to layoffs. Nadella did not answer that question. He said the offer was mostly about giving staff more agency. People can move into roles that make long-term economic sense for them.

“If you’re in a team where you feel stuck professionally, you can vote with your feet,” Nadella said. “I wish I could just sit here and say it’ll all be the same. I cannot.”

Many of those places are inside Microsoft itself, he added. He said not every part of Microsoft had “got the memo” on transforming. Team sizes and workflows will change across the company’s 200,000 people, he added. One of Microsoft’s fastest-growing jobs is the forward-deployed engineer.

On new graduates, Nadella said teams first need to reorganise and build their new “software factories.” Hiring early-career people comes after that. Drawing long-term conclusions from the slowdown now would be “too early,” he said. Microsoft has started a mentoring programme with Carnegie Mellon University, called PRAISE, for engineers early in their careers.

“In a world where code generation has become cheap, what has become hard is verification,” Nadella said.

He said models used to critique code can carry alignment problems, so he favours checking one model family with another. He also wants production traces to feed a loop that verifies fixes, which he called “my RSI.”

Companies should treat AI agents as an “insider risk,” Nadella said. Models are getting more capable, but not more reliable, a point he also made on 20VC last month. He called for audited, tamper-proof logs of how agents reason.

He also told companies to keep their agent software, memory, and models separate, so no vendor locks them in. His test: a firm should be able to swap any model and still improve on its private evaluations.

“If you can’t do that, then you have to ask yourself how are you a sovereign firm,” he said.

Last year’s frontier models can already run on a laptop and last quarter’s on a desktop, Nadella said. He expects routers such as GitHub Copilot Fusion to send some tasks to local models and others to the cloud, which he called the start of a “hybrid intelligence era.” He described local models as “unmetered intelligence.”

His advice to engineers was to spend less time reading about AI and more time using it.

“If I could change the ratio of my talk to do, I would do it. This is the time,” Nadella said.

#3181. macOS 27.3 beta 2 now available with vertical tabs in Safari, native Live Activities, more

Apple is rolling out the second developer beta of macOS 27.3 ahead of the official launch of the update, which includes several notable additions. Here’s what’s coming.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, followed by the public beta a few days later, amid a slew of hardware releases that included new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

And contrary to macOS 27.2, the new update is shaping up to be pretty significant. In addition to expanding Siri AI support to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

macOS 27.3 also introduces Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, as well as native Live Activities support in the menu bar. Additionally, macOS 27.3 so far include native Markdown rendering in Quick Look, a new Pro Light screensaver, and additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links.

#3180. You can now ask Siri AI questions about your health data, with iOS 27.3 beta 2

While Siri AI expanded on what kinds of things you can ask Apple’s voice assistant in many ways, one area where the system took a step back was health data. Since Siri AI’s launch in iOS 27.0, the system has enforced guardrails that do not allow it to access data from the Health app, despite the older Siri Classic being able to do just that.

However, it seems Apple is about to close the gap. In the latest iOS 27.3 beta, just released to developers today, users are now able to ask their iPhone about health data related questions and Siri AI will answer.

For instance, you can ask about your recent step count or heart rate readings, find out about activity rings progress, log medications and more.

When asking Siri for health stats, the assistant generates a human natural language response and renders a little inline card that uses familiar user interface elements from the Health app. Similarly, if you ask about your activity rings, a visualisation of your activity rings is shown in the chat transcript.

Again, this is catch-up compared to what you’ve been able to do with old Siri for several years at this point. However, empowered by the LLM behind the scenes, you can ask questions about your health data that are a bit more open-ended.

You can also do more complicated requests like ‘Send a message to Chance about the status of my activity rings’, or ‘How many steps am I on track to do this week?’. These are the kind of tasks that old Siri would never be able to do.

At least on this current build, the new Siri AI Health functionality appears to have been enabled on iOS. It’s currently unclear if the functionality will also be available through watchOS.

iOS 27.3 also introduces a revamped Health app, with a radically new design that includes new insights, suggestions and views about your health and fitness.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and is expected to be released publicly later this year, likely in early December.

The worst-kept secret in Cupertino is finally spilling out onto the timeline. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is targeting WWDC 2027 to launch its first pair of smart glasses.

Back in 2025, I wrote that visionOS was quietly setting the stage for a killer pair of smart specs — completely sidestepping the bulky, overpriced Apple Vision Pro. Well, turns out that prediction was dead on, as a stripped down version of the OS and an older Apple Watch chip will be packed into a frame thinner than the Ray-Ban Metas.

Sounds like a home run on paper, but there are some big obstacles between now and WWDC to overcome — not just in Apple’s software, but in smart eyewear more broadly.

The most exciting detail about the prototype (codenamed N50) isn’t that “Tic Tac” sized MagSafe charger or the flushed oval cameras — it’s that native Wi-Fi connectivity. Up until this point, anyone wearing smart glasses will know the Bluetooth tether is their Achilles’ heel.

Wearables are supposed to gain you freedom from your phone, and you can’t really do that if you rely on something you have to be close to. The moment you walk into another room leaving your phone on your desk, that wearable turns into a pair of dumb specs.

But by giving the glasses their own Wi-Fi radio, Apple could be granting you actual independence. That friction of leaving your phone on the charger at home and still streaming audio/pinging Siri would be a huge quality-of-life upgrade. The closest we’re getting to this is the cellular data plan in Snap Specs at the moment.

My initial prediction was based on the idea that visionOS is a visual experience. “Vision” is in the name after all, but if you were hoping for AR displays, you’re going to have to keep waiting. According to Gurman, Apple’s first glasses will be a screen-free experience.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With audio and cameras in the driving sign, the glasses will use visual intelligence to scan your surroundings and Siri AI to answer questions about it, all while relying on built-in mics and speakers for calls and Apply Music playback.

Of course, one of the key benefits here is that by ditching the heavy optical engines, Apple gets to keep the glasses lightweight, stylish and comfortable. But also, this design choice creates a massive, singular issue: the future of this category needs a screen (in my opinion).

And this brings me to the elephant in the room. Apple is betting the entire farm on Siri, but Siri’s not ready yet.

The master plan is Siri being the agentic bridge of your devices. Instead of developers building dedicated apps for the glasses, your assistant will just hijack your existing iOS apps — booking Ubers, ordering Starbucks or securing OpenTable reservations entirely through conversation.

In theory, it’s brilliant. In practice, it could be a very tough hill to climb.

Between now and 2027, Siri AI needs to get so much better. Currently, we’re seeing long pause times to simple prompts on your iPhone, and the Apple HomeView routinely fumbles complex, multi-step smart home commands.

If Siri is currently struggling to seamlessly manage a stationary smart home, imagine how badly it is going to hallucinate when you’re walking down a noisy Manhattan street asking it to visually analyze a restaurant menu and cross-reference your calendar.

Gurman’s report already notes that Apple’s software and AI development is running behind schedule, which could easily delay this 2027 launch. And honestly? They should until it’s bulletproof.

Apple’s hardware team looks set to deliver a sleek, Wi-Fi-enabled wearable showpiece. But if they strap it to an AI assistant that still doesn’t understand what you actually want, that expensive pair of smart glasses is going to feel like a very expensive bluetooth headset.

And that’s before even looking at the usability of these agentic flows. Uber reported that AI agents only booked four rides in a week. Four. And there are many more examples. Adoption just isn’t there right now. That’s not to say it shouldn’t happen, but it will take a far smarter Siri graduating to a true agent to make it worthwhile.

#3178. iOS 27.3 brings vertical video and video podcasts to Apple TV app

iOS 27.3 beta 2 debuted today and includes two new types of video in the Apple TV app: vertical ‘clips’ and video podcasts.

The Apple TV app is expanding in two key ways with iOS 27.3, which is now in beta and ships next month.

First, Apple is introducing vertical video through a new ‘clips’ feature.

Similar to what streaming services like Netflix and Disney+ offer, the feature is a way to let users sample short-form previews of Apple TV content in a TikTok-style interface.

Inside the TV app in iOS 27.3, the Home tab has a new section: ‘Explore Clip Collections.’ Currently the collections include themed titles like ‘Absolute Adrenaline,’ ‘Animal Action,’ ‘Close Calls,’ and ‘Mind-Bending Moments.’

Tap to open a collection and you’ll start playing a short-form clip from Apple Originals with the option to swipe vertically to watch other clips. As you’d expect, Apple provides convenient buttons for adding the TV show or movie to your Watchlist.

iOS 27.3 also brings video podcasts from the Apple Podcasts app into TV.

As we reported this morning, there’s a dedicated video podcasts section coming to the TV app. But you can also, via your Account Settings, choose to sync playback data from Apple Podcasts.

If you enable sync, then video podcasts played in one app will be added to the queue and playback history in both apps.

#3175. Microsoft blames its Microsoft 365 outage on a dormant July update defect

Microsoft’s preliminary report says its load tests ran on weaker hardware, so a lock contention bug went unseen. When Teams traffic surged and capacity dropped, the Microsoft 365 outage spread server to server.

Microsoft has traced last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage to a July update for its network gateway servers. The bug lay dormant for more than three months before a surge in load and a drop in capacity set it off, according to the company’s preliminary post-incident report.

Microsoft published the report to customers in the Microsoft 365 admin centre on 15 November, The Register reported. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, agents and platform, posted an abridged version on X on Monday, ZDNET reported.

“A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions,” Lamanna wrote.

The July update was built specifically for the Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. It passed load testing and ran worldwide without problems, Microsoft said. But the defect caused lock contention inside an internal Windows process, which exhausted a server’s CPU and memory.

Testing missed it, because the load tests focused on weaker hardware with fewer cores, according to the report. The contention is worse on newer machines with more cores.

Two other conditions then met. Teams failed over to the gateway that also carries Exchange Online, which raised the load. At the same time, an unrelated issue from the day before had taken nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity out of service.

When a server stopped responding, traffic moved to the next healthy one, which then hit the same bug. Within two hours, more than 80% of the servers were unresponsive at the lowest point, the report says.

Waiting traffic overwhelmed servers again as soon as they came back online. Microsoft said its automated recovery was not designed for such a broad failure.

“Since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change,” Lamanna wrote.

Engineers instead wrote an update that returned the Windows code path to its previous state. They applied it to groups of servers in turn. Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and the Office apps could move off the faulty gateways and came back sooner. Exchange Online could not, for scale reasons, which is why Outlook was down longest.

The report’s timeline, as published by The Register, starts with the Teams failover at 01:07 UTC on 12 November. The first support case came in at 16:33 UTC. Microsoft applied its fix from 07:20 UTC on 13 November and sent its final customer update at 04:15 UTC on 14 November.

More than 1,000 engineers and other staff joined outage calls led by Lamanna and cloud chief Scott Guthrie, Bloomberg reported. On 13 November, Microsoft apologised and said the cause was not a cyberattack or AI agents.

We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.

This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.

Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.

We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete.

— Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026

The outage hit governments, courts, hospitals, and businesses. Downdetector logged reports from 74 countries and territories, according to the Associated Press. TNW covered the restoration of services and Europe’s sovereignty debate that followed.

Last month, a Google Cloud outage in its London region hit services including Revolut.

House Homeland Security Committee chair Andrew Garbarino told Politico he was seeking more information from Microsoft and CISA.

“We need to understand what happened and how to make these systems more resilient,” Garbarino said.

Microsoft plans to publish its final post-incident report on 20 November, according to The Register.

#3171. MagSafe Monday: MOFT’s Trackable Field Wallet holds eight cards, cash, and supports Find My

The one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it shows up in the Find My app.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

MOFT has been making the origami-style folding wallet for many years, and this model works like any other Find My accessory. So that means you get left-behind alerts when you leave without it, and the ability to make it trackable through Apple’s network if it’s across town instead of under the couch. It also works with Google’s Find Hub on Android, which matters if you’ve got a mixed household of devices.

The wallet is powered by a built-in battery rather than a watch-style battery, and MOFT says a charge lasts about six months. You charge it by placing the wallet on a Qi charger for about an hour and a half, which, in practice, means dropping it on a MagSafe dock twice a year. That’s a better setup than an AirTag in a wallet as well.

The wallet holds up to eight cards, or closer to four to six if you also use the hidden compartment for cash. A pull tab in the wallet brings your everyday cards out in one motion, while your driver’s license and cash stay tucked inside of it. It’s made from MOFT’s vegan leather and at 14 mm thick, it’s slimmer than a traditional wallet but noticeably thicker than Apple’s card-only wallet, which is the price you are going to pay to hold up this much stuff.

The stand is the usual MOFT origami fold-out, and it works in portrait and landscape for FaceTime or watching a video on the plane. You can buy it without the stand if you’d rather have the thinner version. It comes in Jet Black, Misty Cove, Terracotta, and Peony.

Two things to know going in. There’s no RFID blocking in this version (MOFT has a non-Find My Snap Field Wallet if you want that). MOFT also warns that the magnets can affect magnetic-stripe cards, so avoid putting a hotel key in it.

I’ve spent the past month on a Pelican accessory beat, using wallets designed for outdoor use. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is the other end of that accessory spectrum: more cards, a stand, and Find My built in. If Find My is the reason you’ve stuck with Apple’s wallet, this is a really nice option that holds a bunch and is trackable.

The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from MOFT.

#3170. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3168. AxoGen: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

The NerveTape acquisition opens a surgical market that represents 40-50% of nerve procedures, a structural expansion beyond its core transplant business.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, AxoGen (AXGN -0.98%) raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to at least $290 million. The company's nerve repair portfolio is gaining broader adoption across surgical specialties. Expanding health plan coverage helps secure its market position.

Management highlights three takeaways that drive this growth.

AxoGen acquired BioCircuit to add NerveTape, a sutureless device that connects severed nerves faster than traditional stitching, to its product line. This acquisition expands the addressable market into direct nerve repairs, which represent nearly half of all surgical nerve transection procedures.

Securing reimbursement coverage from major health plans removes a key barrier to hospital adoption for Avance Nerve Graft, the company's biological nerve transplant product. Near-universal commercial coverage allows surgeons across the country to select nerve reconstruction without administrative delays.

Surgical nerve repair during prostate cancer removal represents a major expansion opportunity. Clinical data showed 80% of patients restored meaningful function after receiving nerve grafts, prompting management to initiate commercial market development in 2027.

Revenue grew 26.2% year over year in the third quarter as surgical demand expanded across target applications. Management is aligning production plans and driving pricing discipline to support long-term gross margins.

Direct sales expansion and clinical evidence creation give the company structural advantages in hospital surgical departments. Management is tracking rep productivity and surgical account expansion while integrating newly acquired technologies.

Robert Pattinson is James Bond. Today (Nov. 16), Amazon MGM Studios confirmed it’s found its new 007 in the form of the British actor most known for his roles as Edward Cullen in “Twilight,” Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series, and for shouting “somebody get these beggars out of here” in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster megahit “The Odyssey.”

In an announcement post on the James Bond website, Pattinson said, “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime.

“I'm deeply grateful to Denis [Villeneuve], Amy [Pascal], David [Heyman], Tanya [Lapointe], and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.

Pattinson succeeds Daniel Craig, who bowed out of Bond with 2021’s “No Time to Die,” his fifth outing as the suave superspy. While there is no release date for Pattinson debut as 007, the next installment in the long-running franchise will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who has already worked with Pattinson on the upcoming “Dune Part 3,” and the next Bond blockbuster will be written by Steven Knight, the creator of “Peaky Blinders.”

On the casting news, which has been the subject of intense media and fan speculation, Mike Hopkins, Head of Prime Video & Amazon MGM Studios, said, “Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond as we proudly introduce Robert Pattinson as the next 007.

“This iconic character has captivated audiences around the world for more than six decades, and there’s no doubt that Robert’s remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice to carry that legacy forward.”

Pattinson is believed to have won out against a competitive field with several other actors under consideration, including Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Nicholas Hoult.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Pattinson will be the seventh actor to portray Ian Fleming's beloved character on the big screen in an Eon Productions-produced 007 film. It will be the 26th James Bond movie in the ongoing franchise; the first was 1962's "Dr. No."

The James Bond casting rumor mill has been in overdrive in recent weeks. And while the odds-on favorite kept switching (first it was Turner, then Lowden), once Pattinson’s name emerged, the wind was only blowing one way.

In many ways, Pattinson was the safe pick. He is the most high-profile star of the names rumored to be in the running, and he has extensive experience working in the Hollywood blockbuster machine, having featured in major franchises like “Twilight,” “Harry Potter” and “The Batman” — the long-delayed sequel to which Pattinson is currently filming.

However, being the safe pick doesn’t make him the wrong choice, far from it. Pattinson is a guaranteed draw. Earlier this year, alongside Zendaya, he helped drive the off-kilter romantic comedy “The Drama” to $135 million globally, a sign that Pattinson can get butts in seats. His latest movie, “Primetime,” has grossed $62 million worldwide on a sub-$15 million budget.

More importantly, Pattinson is beloved by a key demographic that Amazon MGM will hope to court with its next Bond movie: younger viewers. The Bond IP goes far with older watchers, but for the franchise to remain at the top of the Hollywood table, it will need to get the TikTok generation watching. Pattinson is the type of actor who can speak to multiple generations.

So, while some longtime 007 fans will bemoan Amazon’s decision to cast an A-lister instead of taking the approach of Bond’s former stewards, the Broccoli family, by selecting a relative unknown. In 2026, Robert Pattinson looks to tick all the right boxes for a new era of Bond.

#3163. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3161. Apple’s leadership overhaul continues with new Apple Pay and Wallet chief

Bloomberg reports that Apple lifer Corey Fugman will replace Jennifer Bailey as the head of the Apple Pay and Wallet division. Here are the details.

A few months ago, Bloomberg reported that Jennifer Bailey, Apple’s head of Apple Pay and Wallet, who had led Apple Pay since its launch in 2014, would retire in October.

At the time, Apple’s services boss Eddy Cue said internally that the company would announce its succession plan before her transition at the end of October, and that she would “continue to be available to support the transition in an advisory role.”

October came and went without any public announcement on that front. Today, however, Bloomberg reported that Apple has tapped Corey Fugman, “a 26-year company veteran as the new head of its payment service and digital wallet unit.”

According to his LinkedIn profile, Fugman joined Apple in September 2000 as Merchandising Manager for Apple Retail and has held several leadership positions since then, including overseeing Apple Card and Apple Cash from 2019 to 2021.

Most recently, he served as Senior Director of Apple Pay and Wallet, a position he has held since November 2021.

With the new job, Fugman inherits a crucial tap-to-pay business, which is estimated to generate billions of dollars a year. It handles tens of billions of transactions annually across more than 90 markets, with Apple taking a percentage.

The division also includes the Apple Card, which is transitioning from a partnership with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to JPMorgan Chase & Co. Fugman has been highly involved with the shift to Chase, which is still ongoing, the people said.

The report notes that Fugman will report to Cue, and reaffirms that Bailey “will remain a consultant in the coming months,” echoing Cue’s earlier comments about her role in the transition.

Finally, Bloomberg adds that while Apple has undergone several leadership changes in recent months, including John Ternus replacing Tim Cook as CEO, Cue’s responsibilities have expanded considerably.

In addition to overseeing services such as Apple TV, Apple Music, Maps, and iCloud, Cue has recently taken charge of the App Store and Health following Jeff Williams’ departure as Chief Operating Officer and Phil Schiller’s decision to step down from overseeing the App Store.

#3160. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.
