#3158. New iPhone Duo orders now deliver a month earlier than before

Interested in getting an iPhone Duo before Christmas? You might be in luck, as Apple’s online store delivery estimates just got pulled forward by a full month, with December delivery now expected.

Apple seems to be finding success in ramping up its iPhone Duo production.

Within minutes of iPhone Duo pre-orders opening on October 16, delivery estimates quickly slipped into November, then December, and after about a half hour of orders, the earliest you could get an iPhone Duo was late January.

Apple did deliver some Duo units earlier than the initial estimates. But the late January timeframe remained in place for all new iPhone Duo orders until now.

But as spotted by Max Weinbach, new iPhone Duo orders from Apple just got bumped up by about a month. Now, delivery estimates are showing December 16-23 for customers in the US and elsewhere.

New Duo orders seemed to have been pulled forward ~a month They must be scaling manufacturing quickly pic.twitter.com/VFkCmCoRLF

This is a great indicator that Apple has been able to accelerate production. It’s also likely that there was a slowdown in orders due to the late January estimate putting off prospective buyers, thus making it easier for the company to catch up on backorders.

While we still don’t know sales numbers, the iPhone Duo by all appearances has been a hit already. And with iOS 27.3 adding a face unlock feature soon, one of the biggest critiques reviewers had is largely being mitigated.

#3157. Why Nvidia Stock Fell Again

Tuesday's earnings report now has to do more than hit big numbers, because the company also has to reassure investors that the Huang story isn't about to get worse.

Nvidia Corporation (NVDA -4.12%) stock fell once again, finishing Monday, Nov. 16, down 4.1%, as investors continued to digest the ouster of its co-founder, Jensen Huang.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -1.92%) and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -2.49%) sank 1.9% and 2.5%, respectively.

Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and CEO of 33 years, resigned last Thursday after reports broke of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected of spying for China.

Then, over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that he had discussed a comeback with allies. A petition asking for Huang to be reinstated had reached more than 180,000 signatures -- including Elon Musk's -- as of Monday morning.

But earlier today, CNBC reported that the board is not in talks to bring Jensen back and is instead focused on an investigation into whether Huang's conduct compromised national security or company secrets.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board searches for Huang's permanent replacement. She will lead the company's earnings call after the bell on Tuesday.

To say the stakes are high for this one would be an understatement. Wall Street is looking for revenue of $109 billion, or 91% growth. The market was already expecting incredible numbers, but now the company has to reassure investors that the Huang story isn't about to get worse.

#3156. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

Following the arrival of Apple Intelligence on iPhones in China with iOS 27.3 beta 1, Apple is now expanding support to iPads and Macs ahead of the public release of its 27.3 updates. Here are the details.

Apple’s road to releasing Apple Intelligence in China has been a particularly eventful one.

After a significant amount of regulatory back-and-forth, the company confirmed in late October that Apple Intelligence would make its way to iPhones as of iOS 27.3, beginning with the first beta of the system, released in early November.

Just a few days later, Reuters reported that Apple had cleared another regulatory hurdle in the country by registering Apple Intelligence for use on tablets and laptops.

Today, Apple released the second developer betas of iPadOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3, both of which now include Apple Intelligence support in China, as spotted by MacRumors.

As with the initial iPhone rollout in the first iOS 27.3 beta, Apple Intelligence on iPads and Macs in China does not include Siri AI or the other next-generation AI features announced at WWDC 2026.

Instead, users get access to earlier capabilities such as Writing Tools, Genmoji, Live Translation, and notification summaries, with Alibaba’s Qwen model powering certain features.

#3153. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027.

McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

"We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta.

Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the company's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

#3152. ‘Schmigadoon!’ and ‘Widow’s Bay’ land Apple TV two Grammy nominations

Apple TV today celebrated two Grammy nominations, one of which further establishes a canceled show as an unlikely awards success story. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, the Broadway adaptation of Apple TV’s ‘Schmigadoon!’ won four Tony Awards, including Best Musical, making Apple TV an EGOT winner by completing its collection of Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony awards.

‘Schmigadoon!’ premiered on Apple TV in 2021 and ran for two seasons, ending in 2023. In January 2024, show creator Cinco Paul confirmed that, although the third season had already been written with 25 new songs, Apple decided not to move forward with it.

Even before the Broadway adaptation’s Tony wins in June, a May report had raised hopes for the show’s return, revisiting an earlier interview in which ‘Schmigadoon!’ creator Cinco Paul revealed that there had been discussions about reviving it.

While there have been no further updates on a potential revival since then, fans got another reason to celebrate today, as the Broadway cast recording of ‘Schmigadoon!’ has been nominated for Best Musical Theater Album at the 2027 Grammy Awards.

It will compete against CHESS the Musical, The Lost Boys, Ragtime, and Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York).

Additionally, ‘Widow’s Bay‘ earned a nomination for Best Score Soundtrack for Visual Media, putting composer David Fleming up against the soundtracks of ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘One Battle After Another,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and ‘Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu‘.

The 2027 Grammy Awards will take place on Sunday, February 7, 2027. To check out the full list of nominees, follow this link.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

#3150. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

The Former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair makes a scary prediction

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There seems to be a slew of warning signs pointing to the inevitability of the AI bubble bursting a lot sooner than most people think.

The controversial ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (who happens to be recognized as the "high priest" of the global AI buildout) and the stock market volatility tied to companies that have made huge investments in AI are two of the bigger signs pointing to the AI bubble bursting. Plus, there have been plenty of major personalities in the tech and business worlds who have given their thoughts on it becoming a reality at some point.

One of those individuals is the Former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair, Gary Gensler, who sat down with CNN to give his own take on the possibility of the AI burst event coming to fruition.

Here’s what he had to say and why his prediction places it near the next presidential election.

Gensler, who ran the Securities and Exchange Commission from 2021 until 2025, told CNN that today’s AI infrastructure buildout has already crossed into bubble territory and will likely lead into a recession before the next presidential election. "It's already a bubble," the former Wall Street regulator stated. "The only question is if it's a soft recession or something more dramatic."

On the topic of all the big spending dedicated to strengthening the current AI infrastructure (which is said to have reached $800 billion a year by some estimates), Gensler pointed to past trends where major investments in technology eventually stagnate.

“History tells us that when you have a new technology and a significant investment ... you come to a point where it plateaus. It retrenches,” Gensler noted. “The only question is if it’s a soft recession or something more dramatic.” The previous instances he cited as big tech investments that eventually met steep declines included railroads, 1920s electricity and the 1990s dot-com boom.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

As for when he sees the AI bubble bursting, he points to it going down sometime before the next presidential election. "I think we're going to have this repricing and a softening of the economy that happens before November 2028," he went on to say. "I can't say exactly when and how stormy, but I would be battening down some hatches."

Gensler is among the many other voices in the tech and investment industries who have given their thoughts on the possibilities of the AI bubble bursting and the resulting fallout. Gary Marcus, the former head of AI for Uber, argued to the Financial Times that today’s AI boom is a massive financial bubble driven by unsustainable economics and technological dead ends:

“If there is a deflation of the AI bubble, the optimists say that the new infrastructure will remain even if the companies do not — just as railways survived the 19th-century railway bust. However, this fails to reckon with the reality of depreciation (few pieces of silicon hold their value for very long because better chips inevitably come along) and the possibility that LLMs could be displaced by more efficient models less dependent on massive numbers of expensive AI chips. In placing massive hyperscaling bets, investors are setting lavish expectations about future earnings. But LLMs are not likely to replicate the near monopolies that have made the market power of current tech giants hard to assail. A better analogy for them might be airlines, which are hobbled by small margins, intense competition, high expenses and dependence on hardware created by outside vendors.” – @garymarcus in @FinancialTimesJune 26, 2026

The Canadian mining financier Frank Giustra was quite frank with his AI bubble burst prediction while speaking at this year’s New Orleans Investment Conference. “There will be a reckoning, and some of these companies will get destroyed," he said. During that same conversation, investor Grant Williams compared the disconnect between recognizing the stock market dangers attached to AI investments and taking proper precautions to a natural disaster.

"If we told you a hurricane was heading to New Orleans, everybody would take precautions," he explained. "The interesting thing about stock market bubbles is people don't really think about what can go wrong. They're still thinking about making money."

While many voices are speaking on the very real possibility of an AI bubble burst, there are business bigwigs who have made it clear that everyone shouldn’t be all that worried about it. During a sit-down interview with CNBC, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos tried to ease everyone’s fears about such a financially devastating event coming to pass. “Even if it does turn out to be a bubble, you shouldn’t worry about it because the bubble is driving investment and a lot of the investment is going to turn out to be very healthy,” he proclaimed.

Bret Taylor, the chairman of OpenAI and CEO of Sierra, spoke to The Verge and flat-out acknowledged that an AI bubble exists while still noting that it's totally fine. And while speaking to CNBC at the 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, his AI optimism pointed to a scenario where the market will correct itself as weaker industry players and overfunded ventures will fall by the wayside.

“When everyone knows that AI is going to have a huge impact on the economy across a huge range of industries and workflows, money is plentiful,” Taylor noted. “I think over the next few years, you’ll see a correction, you also see consolidation, but I don’t think you can get innovation without that kind of messy competition.”

Gensler’s prophetic words about the AI bubble bursting before we even reach the next presidential election are alarming, yes.

But I can envision a world where potential candidates use that moment as one of their political talking points in a bid to ease back on all that AI spending, put more into the American populace and hold back on bailing out any of the AI companies that are hurting from such a traumatic event.

All signs point to something devastating happening to the AI industry at some point, especially with the huge backlash against data centers and the politicians who are looking to put in moratoriums on their continued development.

Elton Jones covers AI for Tom’s Guide, and tests all the latest models, from ChatGPT to Gemini to Claude to see which tools perform best — and how they can improve everyday productivity.

He is also an experienced tech writer who has covered video games, mobile devices, headsets, and now artificial intelligence for over a decade. Since 2011, his work has appeared in publications including The Christian Post, Complex, TechRadar, Heavy, and ONE37pm, with a focus on clear, practical analysis.

Today, Elton focuses on making AI more accessible by breaking down complex topics into useful, easy-to-understand insights for a wide range of readers.

#3145. Stock Market Today, Nov. 16: Tech Selloff Deepens as AI Leadership Crisis Rattles Nasdaq

Investors weighed a Nvidia leadership shakeup, rising Treasury yields, and fresh chip export curbs as tech stocks slid across the board, today, Nov. 16, 2026.

Falling 2.49% to 24,510, the Nasdaq Composite plunged as technology sentiment soured, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.92% to 7,416 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -1.41%) lost 1.41% to 51,608 as selling pressure expanded across the market.

Gold fell 0.88% to $3,852.10 as of U.S. market close, while the 10-Year Treasury yield rose to 5.15% (+0.05%) as Real Estate outperformed relative to laggards in Communication Services and Technology.

Tyson Foods, Inc. shares surged 8.72% after the company exceeded quarterly earnings expectations and provided a positive outlook for its beef segment, but the broader market was weighed down by Nvidia Corporation, which fell 4.12% amid a leadership crisis. Elsewhere, Intel Corporation dropped 7.02% during a volatile session for semiconductors, and Dell Technologies Inc. slid 6.96% following warnings about industrywide debt.

Today was a challenging day for tech stocks, with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ -2.67%) falling 2.66% to $661.84 per share. This drop occurred as negative sentiment hit the sector on multiple fronts.

Aside from the ongoing struggles with Nvidia's leadership crisis, AMD stock suffered due to new export restrictions on advanced AI chips to Southeast Asian countries. Consequently, the stock fell by 5.58% to $504.28 per share.

Moreover, Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman turned hawkish on corporate debt levels. This is concerning to hyperscalers like Meta Platforms, which depend heavily on debt financing to fund their AI build-outs.

Furthermore, the tech sector faces further tests this week when Nvidia announces its earnings for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 on Tuesday after the bell. This is Nvidia's first earnings call without CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, and the announcement could offer hints on the company's direction going forward.

Additionally, Anthropic's IPO is set for Thursday. The company is set to price its IPO on Wednesday night, and how it performs Thursday and industry sentiment could influence its performance.

Indeed, investors face an unusual amount of uncertainty, though it is possible Nvidia's earnings report and Anthropic's IPO could ease some of those doubts. Knowing that, watching and waiting may be an AI investor's best strategy for now.

#3144. Former Apple chairman Arthur Levinson files to sell $31.8 million in company stock

Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the company.

Today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

#3142. Is Moderna's Cancer Vaccine a Game Changer for the Stock?

The healthcare stock has hit multi-year highs this year amid positive results from its personalized cancer vaccine.

The market has been wildly excited about Moderna (MRNA -3.63%) this year, as it has soared more than 600% since January. The stock has been red hot on news that the cancer vaccine it has been working on with healthcare giant Merck has been shown to be highly effective in clinical trials.

Moderna's market cap has swelled to close to $90 billion, up from less than $12 billion at the start of 2026. Is the company's cancer vaccine truly a game changer for Moderna, or is hype and speculation fueling its returns this year?

On Aug. 19, Moderna announced phase 3 clinical trial results that would send its stock skyrocketing. The results showed that its cancer vaccine, intismeran was highly effective in treating melanoma patients when paired with Keytruda, Merck's top cancer drug. The combined treatment reduced the risk of death and of the cancer spreading or coming back, and was more effective than Keytruda on its own.

While approval hasn't happened yet, it does appear highly likely. But there are multiple things to consider here. The stock's mammoth price movement may appear to price in the potential for intismeran to treat other cancers as well, which is by no means a certainty. Plus, producing a personalized cancer vaccine at significant scale can be costly and time-consuming. And with the companies splitting the profits on the treatment, that will also diminish just how much profit may flow through to Moderna's bottom line in the long run.

This is why, although the treatment is incredibly promising and could unlock significant growth potential for Moderna, many investors may have bid the stock up too aggressively, pushing its valuation to an unsustainable level.

Intismeran has the potential to certainly be a game changer for Moderna, but it's not there yet. It's not approved to treat a single cancer, and the stock appears priced as if it'll treat several.

The danger is that investors appear to be getting ahead of themselves and paying too much for the healthcare stock when there are still so many question marks about just how profitable intismeran will be, given the operational challenges that will come with producing a personalized cancer vaccine at scale.

I wouldn't buy Moderna's stock at its current price point, as it may be approaching a peak, if it hasn't already hit one. The stock could have considerable downside risk at this point.

Following the rollout of Siri AI to select Apple TV models with tvOS 27.2.1, Apple today expanded availability to users running the tvOS 27.3 developer beta. Here are the details.

Last Friday, Apple released tvOS 27.2.1, bringing the new Siri AI to Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and 3rd-gen models. The feature requires a nearby, paired device with Siri AI enabled.

The update came just hours after the official launch of the Apple TV 4K (4th generation), which ships with Siri AI support out of the box.

However, users running tvOS 27.3 beta 1 still had no access to the new Siri AI. This means that although the feature was available in the latest public release, users on the beta were left without it.

Earlier tonight, Apple released tvOS 27.3 beta 2, which, as leaker pdfu noted in a post on X, now includes a new setup screen inviting users to enable Siri AI.

New Siri AI upsell screen on tvOS 27.3 beta 2. pic.twitter.com/VIunVgCptG

9to5Mac was able to confirm the change, with the new splash screen introducing Siri AI and giving users the option to try the new assistant or continue using Siri Classic.

With Siri AI now available on both the public and beta versions of tvOS, the new HomePod mini 2 is still waiting for the feature. Apple previously confirmed that Siri AI would arrive in a future software update, but it was not included in last Friday’s HomePod 27.2.1 release, and the company has yet to announce a rollout date.

#3139. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 stocks for the long haul

Global stock markets have been volatile as investors assess high bond yields and continued tensions between the U.S. and Iran. There are concerns about the impact of uncertainty in the Middle East on oil prices and consequently on inflation.

Investors who prefer to look beyond short-term noise and buy stocks with attractive long-term growth potential can follow the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts. The ratings of these experts are backed by in-depth research of a company's financials and thorough analysis of the factors affecting its business performance.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Semiconductor giant Nvidia (NVDA) reported stellar fiscal second-quarter results and reassured investors about continued strength in AI-driven demand for its chips. Moreover, Nvidia's FY28 revenue growth outlook of 70% was well above the Street's expectations.

Reacting to the Q2 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore reiterated a buy rating on NVDA and increased his price target to $300 from $288. "This is our Top Pick in the semis group, with a compelling product cycle, exceptional growth and valuation below peers," said the 5-star analyst.

Nvidia delivered impressive quarterly results despite supply constraints, Moore said, but he believes that the FY28 revenue and gross margin commentary mattered more, with a favorable outlook for both measures.

Moore said Nvidia's 70% revenue growth guidance for FY28 was above his own estimate of 52% and the consensus of about 40%. The top-line growth estimate was a "remarkable figure" given supply issues and Moore said he expects Nvidia to continue to address bottlenecks to deliver rapid growth.

Among other takeaways, the analyst said performance metrics for Vera Rubin chips were strong, with Nvidia emphasizing a 30x higher throughput per megawatt and 35x lower token cost compared with Grace Blackwell Ultra.

Moore ranks No. 159 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 24.60%. See Nvidia Statistics on TipRanks.

Ride-hailing and delivery platform Uber Technologies (UBER) was recommended by BMO Capital analyst Brian Pitz, who discussed the company's opportunity in the autonomous vehicle (AV) market in a recent research note that reiterated a buy rating and price target of $119.

The 5-star analyst highlighted Uber's transition into a diversified marketplace, with investors now focusing on its AV growth prospects. The key question is how much value can Uber generate as AVs become commercialized, Pitz asked.

"We continue to believe that Uber's AV strategy is evolving and will become a significant driver of revenue and profitability," the analyst said.

Importantly, Pitz believes that Uber can establish itself as a preferred mobility platform for AV makers, supported by its growing AV infrastructure capabilities and an expanding partner base. This would enable Uber to win a significant share of value as the AV market is commercialized.

Additionally, Pitz noted Uber's enhanced position in the AV value chain, with the company shifting from serving as a distribution channel for robotaxis to becoming a broader platform for AV mobility. The analyst discussed Uber's efforts to capture growth opportunities in the AV market, including higher capital spending, expansion into new markets and building partnerships beyond Alphabet's Waymo.

Pitz ranks No. 574 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of about 12.20%. See Uber Technologies Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Semiconductor company Marvell Technology (MRVL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the second quarter of FY27. But the company's increased FY28 guidance fell short of investors' high expectations.

In reaction to the Q2 FY27 results, KeyBanc analyst John Vinh reaffirmed a buy rating on Marvell Technology, with a price target of $400. The analyst noted that Marvell's results and outlook were driven by strength in its data center business. The Q2 FY27 data center business grew 46% year-over-year, to $2.17 billion, far above KeyBanc's estimate of $2.09 billion.

Management "highlighted accelerating AI networking demand across scale-out, scale-across and scale-up architectures, supported by strong 800G optical DSP demand, rapid 1.6T ramp, broader 51.2T switch deployments and higher TIA/driver demand," Vinh said.

Consequently, Marvell raised its data center revenue guidance, now expecting 60% growth in FY27 and more than 60% in FY28.

Regarding the recently announced $120 billion warrant arrangement with Google, Vinh said management argued that programs tied to the warrant are already priced into the custom outlook through FY28. Meanwhile, new programs and those in execution are expected to drive significant upside to the previous FY29 custom XPU revenue estimate of over $10 billion, Vinh said, citing management.

Vinh ranks No. 123 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 28.50%. See Marvell Technology Technical Analysis on TipRanks.
