#3138. Cycurion (CYCU) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Margins surged, yet a going concern warning still looms.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Cycurion, Inc. (CYCU -6.99%) reported record quarterly revenue and gross profit, driven by the integration of recent acquisitions and a return to organic growth in its core business. Management stated that the company is shifting its strategic focus toward predictive and offensive cybersecurity capabilities, intended to address the widening gap between vulnerability discovery and remediation. The company reported a 40% year-over-year increase in revenue and significant gross margin expansion to 36%. CFO Garcia indicated that the path to profitability relies on growing gross profit faster than operating expenses, supported by a transition toward higher-margin recurring revenue services. The company expects to begin work on a $54.6 million state government contract in early 2027 while continuing to integrate the Digital Ally and Secuvant acquisitions.

Operator: Welcome to Cycurion's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Participants are in listen-only mode. Following prepared remarks, management will address questions submitted in advance. Joining us today are Kevin Kelly, Chief Executive Officer, Ana Garcia, Chief Financial Officer, and Danny White, Chief Product Officer. I would now like to turn it over to Angela Wier, Chief Administrative Officer. Please go ahead.

Angela Wier: Good morning. Today's discussion covers the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Our earnings release and supporting financial information are available on our website at investors.cycurion.com. This call, including the question and answer session, include forward-looking statements about our strategy, products, business outlook, and market opportunities, financing needs, and future plans. We do not provide financial guidance, and nothing on today's call should be taken as guidance. These statements reflect our current expectations and involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Those risks include our ability to obtain capital, meet our obligations, execute contracts, integrate acquisitions, and commercialize our offerings.

For more information, please review the risk factors and other disclosures on our annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, and our subsequent quarterly reports on Form 10-Q filed with the SEC. These statements speak only as of today, November 16, 2026. Kevin, over to you.

Kevin Kelly: Thank you very much, Angie. Good morning, everybody. On behalf of all of our colleagues at Cycurion, we are very happy to have our first earnings call today, so welcome. This was a breakout quarter for Cycurion. Revenue was up $5.4 million, up $1.5 million or 40% from the third quarter of last year, and ahead of the analyst Wall Street consensus estimate of approximately $4.37 million. Profitability improved even faster. Gross margin expanded to approximately 36% from 7% a year ago, and gross profit grew more than sevenfold to approximately $1.9 million from approximately $300,000.

Our adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed by about 64% to approximately $1.2 million from $3.3 million, and our GAAP net loss improved 4% to approximately $3.1 million from $3.2 million. We delivered that growth by delivering higher margin revenue that translated into more gross profit, and we narrowed our operating and adjusted EBITDA losses. The businesses we acquired contributed approximately $1.2 million of the year-over-year increase, and our existing businesses added approximately $300,000, a return to organic growth after project roll-off earlier this year. We are not done. We are very encouraged by this progress and focus on carrying it forward.

Ana Garcia will cover our financial performance, balance sheet, and liquidity, but this quarter shows that our model is working, more revenue, better margins, and disciplined costs. Let me talk about what is driving that momentum and where we are going to go from here. in October, we announced our move into predictive intelligence. Here is the problem that we solve. Imagine a security team that may see a vulnerable application, an unusual login, and intelligence about an attacker as three separate events. We connect those signals to the systems the client depends on and identify which potential attack deserves attention first.

That is the difference, helping clients get ahead of attacks using the context of their own operations rather than only reacting after something happens. It complements detection and response with an earlier view of where that action is and how we can help reduce that risk. Our team brings firsthand experience in how adversaries operate, and that experience shapes how we will build these capabilities. On November 4, we launched Habit, our AI-driven security operations center, which is a concrete step in that direction. Danny White is going to walk through this whole portfolio in just a few minutes. We have built a portfolio with complementary capabilities and customer relationships, and we are now connecting them.

Axxum and Cloudburst are our federal contracting foundation. SLG adds government IT delivery experience and established agency relationships. Together, they give us a direct path to bring more cybersecurity capability to clients who already trust us. Secuvant brought Panoptic and cybersecurity risk management. That is an expertise we can now offer across the entire group. Digital Ally adds video and evidence technology and relationships with more than 800 public safety organizations. That gives us a significant opportunity to bring our cybersecurity offering to those agencies. Our integration plan connects these relationships with each business's capability, coordinates sales, and improves delivery efficiency.

That is how the acquisition portfolio becomes a stronger combined business, and you can already see the contribution in this quarter's results. We have added professionals from the U.S. intelligence community and special operations community, alongside experienced private sector cybersecurity and product leaders. Their experience gives us an edge in two ways. It sharpens how we assess attack behavior, and it gives us a deep understanding of customers whose missions cannot tolerate any disruption. Our product and technology leaders also bring a track record of taking capabilities from development to commercial release, which is extremely important as we go forward. That expertise, combined with a federal contracting base, positions us well for the missions that we are pursuing.

We have clear opportunities to grow the businesses we already own by winning new customers and expanding the work we do for the existing ones. That includes contract renewals and extensions, new government opportunities, and adding products and services for existing clients. We are also building commercial opportunities in sectors such as healthcare and financial services. Cross-selling across the group is a big part of that plan. A public safety customer using our video and evidence systems also needs to protect the environment around those systems, and that is a natural fit for our cybersecurity services.

Selective acquisitions remain part of our strategy, and we look for companies that add capability or customer access with sound earnings and cash profiles, manageable integration, and a funding structure that makes sense for all shareholders. Our priority is growing what we own, and any additional acquisition has to strengthen that plan. Our path to profitability is straightforward. Grow gross profit faster and watch our costs as we're doing that. This quarter shows that is happening. We are focused on higher-margin client work, more product and recurring revenue service, and disciplined delivery and overhead costs as we scale.

Looking into the fourth quarter, we expect to benefit from the initial commercialization of Habit following its November 4 launch, work on our $54.6 million state Health and Human Services contract, which is expected to begin at the end of the first quarter of 2027. Our focus remains the same. Grow gross profit faster than the cost needed to support it, and expand product and recurring revenue, and continue to narrow our losses. We will report progress through gross profit, operating expenses, GAAP results, adjusted EBITDA, and operating cash flow so shareholders can track each milestone along the way to our profitability. I'm going to now turn the call over to Danny White, our Chief Product Officer.

By way of background, Danny came to us through the acquisition of Secuvant and has made huge inroads and has been instrumental in getting these products to market. Danny, thank you.

Danny White: Thank you, Kevin. Before I walk through the portfolio, I want to quickly set the stage on what's happening in the industry and why we feel strongly about our product strategy. For most of its history, cybersecurity has been a defensive discipline. Organizations put up controls, collect alerts, respond after something gets through, but that model is breaking under the speed of modern attacks. Recently, Rapid7, their 2026 Global Threat Landscape Report found that the median time from a vulnerability's disclosure to confirmed exploitation fell from 8.5 days to five days.

Over that same period, Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that the median time for organizations to fully remediate the known exploited vulnerabilities rose from 32 days to 43. Attackers are moving in days, but defenders are still moving in weeks. A purely defensive posture cannot close that gap. The market is starting to recognize this. Gartner projects that by 2030, preemptive security will make up half of all IT security spending, and that is up from less than 5% in 2024. The shift is away from detecting and responding and toward anticipating and acting first. That shift is why our portfolio looks the way it does.

Every security leader we talk to asks three questions: Where am I exposed? What is happening in my environment right now? What is most likely to happen next? Most of the industry answers the first two with separate tools that don't talk to each other, and very few answer the third. We built a product for each question, and we built them to work together. That lets our clients move from a defensive posture to an offensive one, thinking like the attacker and acting before the attack. We tested that thesis in the market.

In August, our team went to Black Hat in Las Vegas, the industry's largest gathering of security vendors and practitioners, and what we saw confirmed our direction. Most of the market was still focused on using AI to help security teams close alerts faster, which is still reacting. Very few vendors were combining exposure, live threat activity, and telemetry into one contextual view, and fewer still were using active testing to prove that a fix worked. Those gaps are exactly where we have focused and how Cycurion stands apart. With that context, our product portfolio is built around those three question areas: exposure, active threats, and the predictive view.

First, we have Panoptic, which covers exposure and is in production today. It identifies vulnerabilities across the client's environment, then ranks cyber risk by asset, threat vector, and exploitability, so clients know where to act first. Panoptic serves customers across multiple industries, from organizations with about $1 million in annual revenue to those with greater than $2 billion. We are in late-stage development of Panoptic 2.0, which adds enhancements and integration with our other two products. Our next product is Habit, which covers active threats. We launched Habit on November 4th as our AI-driven security operations center. Habit learns what normal activity looks like for each client and surfaces deviations.

It combines AI-assisted triage with around-the-clock human analysts, offensive testing, and verification that any fix made actually worked. Lastly, Fathom brings the portfolio together as our integrated predictive intelligence platform, targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Fathom will unify exposure and active threat intelligence with telemetry and operations into a single predictive view to equip organizations with actionable information, allowing them to act before attacks become disruptions. We are also deploying the Cycurion Pulse Technology Modernization Assessment through SLG to help public sector clients with the difficult challenge of modernizing their infrastructure and security investments. Our focus now is execution, turning these products into customer adoption and revenue.

That starts with converting the Habit launch into paid pilots and production deployments. Our commercial strategy is built to scale through MSP agreements, channel partnerships, competitive pricing, and cross-product integration that makes each product more valuable alongside the others. The coming months will set the pace. Habit is in the market now. Panoptic 2.0 releases in mid-December. In the first quarter of 2027, Fathom brings them together into that single predictive view. Each milestone stands on its own, and each one makes the next stronger. In an industry that has spent years trying to help defenders respond faster, we are focused on something different, giving organizations the ability to see what comes next and act before it happens.

That is where the market is going, and we intend to be the company that defines it. Cybersecurity has spent decades reacting to the last attack, but Cycurion is building for the next one. As we move forward, we will continue to report on adoption and revenue contribution for everything that we have mentioned here today. Thank you. Ana, over to you.

Ana Garcia: Thank you, Danny. We are pleased to report record revenue and gross profit for the third quarter of 2026. I will review the quarter's financial results, followed by our results for the first nine months of 2026, and then cover the balance sheet and liquidity. Third quarter revenue increased 40% year-over-year to $5.4 million, beating Wall Street consensus estimate of $4.37 million. Acquisitions contributed $1.2 million to the growth, while organic growth from our existing project pipeline contributed $300,000. Gross profit reached $1.9 million, more than seven times the $300,000 reported in the prior year quarter. Gross margin expanded to 36% compared with 7% a year ago, reflecting contributions from higher-margin acquisitions and profitable deals.

Our reported net loss was $3.1 million compared with $3.2 million in the prior year quarter. The prior year result benefited from a one-time $2 million debt settlement gain. Excluding that non-recurring gain from the prior year comparison, net loss improved 41% year-over-year. Net loss attributable to Cycurion was $2.9 million, or $1.03 per basic and diluted share, compared to $3.1 million, or $12.39 per basic share, and $12.36 per diluted share. Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to approximately $1.2 million from $3.3 million in the prior year quarter, an improvement of 64%. Please refer to the reconciliation to GAAP to net loss in our press release.

Turning to the first nine months of 2026, total company revenue was approximately $12.4 million, up 7% from $11.6 million in the prior year period. Acquisitions contributed $1.3 million to revenue growth, partially offset by early year project roll-offs, with the third quarter returning to organic growth. For the first nine months of 2026, gross profit more than tripled to approximately $3.7 million from $1.2 million in the prior year period. Gross margin expanded to approximately 30% from 10% of the prior year period. Reported net loss improved 48% to approximately $9.7 million from $18.8 million.

For a comparison, excluding non-recurring items, we excluded the debt settlement loss in 2026 and the debt settlement gain and business combination expenses in 2025. On that basis, year-to-date net loss improved 11% to $7.8 million from $8.8 million last year. For the first nine months of 2026, adjusted EBITDA loss was $4.6 million, compared with $4.1 million in the same period last year, reflecting public company costs, SLG consolidation, key growth hires, and the two 2026 acquisitions, which were partly offset by third quarter revenue growth and improved gross margin.

Turning to the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with net debt, that is total debt minus cash and cash equivalents, of $5.3 million, compared with $5.2 million in the prior year quarter and $2.8 million as of December 31, 2025. The increase primarily reflected a $4.3 million promissory note issued for the acquisition of Kustom's video solutions business. This was partially offset by the conversion of a substantial portion of our other notes into common stock during the months of July and August of 2026. Those conversions reduced our obligations, but increased our share count. Turning to liquidity, we ended the quarter with $3 million in cash.

That compares with $1.9 million as of June 30, 2026, and $3.7 million as of June 30, 2025. During the quarter, we raised $4.5 million in gross proceeds through a warrant inducement transaction with an existing investor. We used $1.5 million of those proceeds to fund accretive acquisitions and the remainder to support working capital needs. As disclosed in the company's quarterly report on Form 10-Q, we continue to face going concern uncertainty. We ended the quarter with a working capital deficit of $10.5 million, up from $8.9 million as of December 31, 2025, driven mainly by the promissory note for the Cycurion Digital Ally acquisition and higher accounts payable tied to growth and public company costs.

Third quarter revenue growth, improved gross margin, lower debt following note conversions, and higher receivables and inventory partially offset the increase. Our improving results are helping narrow our funding gap. However, we will continue to need capital to support operations, meet our obligations, and execute on our plan. In closing, we delivered record revenue and gross profit, higher gross margins, and narrower third quarter net and adjusted EBITDA losses. Acquisitions and organic revenue drove these results. Our plan is simple: execute with discipline, cut losses, and keep driving toward profitability. Kevin, back to you.

Kevin Kelly: Thanks, Ana. I want to address financing and dilution directly. We know shareholders care about dilution, and so do we. Equity and convertible financing can increase the share count, and conversions that reduce our debt also affect existing shareholders. We will need additional capital, and our approach is to choose the best option realistically available, weighing pricing, fees, conversion terms, repayment obligations, and potential dilution. Capital should support specific operating objectives, including client delivery, product commercialization, and management of existing obligations. The best answer to dilution is performance. As our results and cash generation improve, we expect our dependence on outside capital to decline over time.

We will explain the financing decisions we make and be held accountable for how that capital is used. Looking ahead, we will build on this quarter's momentum with three clear priorities: completing the integration of Digital Ally, starting work on and ramping the Health and Human Services contract, and turning our predictive intelligence products, starting with the Habit launch, into paying customers. We will measure progress through product adoption, growth in our existing businesses, integration milestones, and continued improvement in gross profit and cash flows. We have brought together the people, customer relationships, and cybersecurity capabilities to build a stronger Cycurion. This quarter is evidence that our strategy is working, and we're focused on building on this foundation.

We'll now turn to the questions that shareholders submitted in advance.

Angela Wier: Hey, Kevin. We will begin with the first question submitted for our leadership team, which is, how is Cycurion approaching financing and further dilution?

Kevin Kelly: Thanks, Angie. Our priority is to secure capital and on the strongest terms, with minimizing dilution and protecting long-term shareholder value. As I mentioned a minute ago, we completely understand shareholders' concerns about dilution, and that weighs directly on our financing decisions. Today, the micro-cap market is our primary source of capital, but at the same time, we're working to broaden our options, including conventional bank funding, which we are targeting for the first quarter of 2027, subject to the lender approval and final terms. As you recall, and we disclosed this a few months ago, we also have a board approval share repurchase program that we intend to use.

As our financial position strengthens, that gives us an additional tool to help offset dilution and return value to shareholders. Any repurchases, as we mentioned before, will also depend on available cash, market conditions, and our capital needs and financing obligations. The capital we are pursuing now is intended to support contract delivery, bring the products to market that I mentioned, and meet our commitments as we position the business for 2027, which we expect to be a great year. Every financing decision has to be evaluated against both its cost to shareholders and the value we expect that capital to create.

Angela Wier: Thank you, Kevin. Ana, the second question is, what is the road to profitability for Cycurion?

Ana Garcia: Yes. Hi. Thanks, Angie. Our path to profitability is straightforward. We are going to grow gross profit faster than operating expenses. We have invested in the people, the products, and the processes needed to do that. Our focus now is converting those investments into financial results. On people, our leadership team is focused on winning profitable business and expanding client relationships. On products, we're bringing offensive and predictive cybersecurity capabilities to market that can increase our contribution from higher-margin revenue. On process, we're strengthening delivery, financial discipline, and cost control as we grow. We are seeing increased business development activity as we finish Q4 of 2026 and enter into 2027.

The next step is converting that activity into signed contracts, revenue, and cash collections. That is the execution agenda: profitable growth, a stronger revenue mix, and disciplined spending. Shareholders will be able to access our progress through our margins, adjusted EBITDA, and operating cash flow.

Angela Wier: Thank you, Ana. Kevin, can you speak to where the organic growth will come from?

Kevin Kelly: Absolutely. For us at Cycurion, this is a tremendous opportunity. If you look what we added in terms of the individuals from the intelligence community, the acquisition of both Secuvant and Digital Ally, we brought in a number of new clients, and also a number of new opportunities. We will see tremendous growth through cross-selling our new products into those clients, as well as we have had some great clients that have stuck with us through the years. The ability now to broaden those clients and expand with our new products is a huge opportunity.

If you look at our portfolio, Pulse, Habit, and Panoptic, these capabilities give us a lot of different ways to address customer needs, and our move towards predictive intelligence is a clear differentiating factor. Digital Ally brings relationships, as we mentioned before, with over 800 public safety organizations. We see opportunities already to grow this business and introduce additional cybersecurity capabilities, where there is clear customer demand. We are also pursuing a number of national security opportunities. Our team includes professionals with backgrounds in U.S. special operations, the intelligence community, bringing both operational experience and mission expertise to our technology capabilities. We are pursuing potential contracts across defense and other government organizations as we speak.

Across all three areas, the objectives are the same: convert our capabilities and relationships into recurring business at higher gross profit and stronger cash generation.

Angela Wier: Thank you, Kevin. Danny, can you speak to what makes predictive intelligence strategy different?

Danny White: Absolutely. Thanks for the question. It actually gets right to the core of who we are. Predictive intelligence means taking the tools and information organizations already have and combining them with the advancements that we are building to give them more context than they have ever had before. With that context, we are able to look at cybersecurity through a new lens. Predictive intelligence does not mean discarding traditional security practices. We combine where a client is exposed, what attackers are actively exploiting, and what is happening in their environment right now to see which attack is most likely to come next based on signal intelligence. The industry, as I mentioned before, is still helping organizations respond to attacks.

Predictive intelligence is really helping them to get ahead of attacks before they happen, and that is exactly what makes our focus on predictive intelligence strategy different.

Angela Wier: Thank you, Danny. The fifth question is, how do acquisitions fit into your growth strategy? Kevin?

Kevin Kelly: Thanks. Since becoming public, we have often said that our ambition is to build on what we've had and to create a $100 million cybersecurity business through a combination of organic growth and acquisitions. Our intended mix is going to be heavily skewed towards the inorganic growth of acquisitions, and we believe that we have a tremendous opportunity there. It's a highly fragmented industry, the cybersecurity industry as a whole, and we're looking at numerous companies, but they have to fit in with our strategic plan and directly what we want to become and grow into as an organization. We're looking for acquisitions that add relevant technology, customer relationships, and credible contribution of profitability.

We evaluate the purchase price, financing costs, shareholder impact, and the work required to integrate each business. We also aspire to grow the corporate side or the commercial side of this business as well, where margins are much higher and the decision-making is much faster. Scale definitely matters, but the quality of that growth matters just as much. Our objective is to build a stronger, more profitable company that creates and delivers greater value to customers and our shareholders.

Angela Wier: Thank you, Kevin. The last question was if Cycurion could provide a general update on the status of ongoing litigation.

Kevin Kelly: Sure. Trying to strike the balance of what we can and can't convey, I would say that this is still in progress. As you recall, after the fake press release that went out on March 16th of this year, it takes time. It takes time. As you recall from the press releases, we have subpoenaed over 18 market makers, and it takes a lot of time to go through those individual trades and records for those days. But stay tuned, that's still in progress, and we will share any new updates with you as they become available.

Angela Wier: Great. Thank you. Kevin, do you have any other remarks?

Kevin Kelly: Yeah. I mean, first of all, in my closing, I'd really like to thank all of our investors out there for staying with us and being patient. We know as a team at Cycurion, we have a tremendous opportunity in front of us. We're starting to make great strides, and we predict that 2027 is going to be a great year. Also, I would like to say I appreciate all of the emails I get and the feedback from the shareholders out there and the input they have. It doesn't pass us by that they have some good remarks, good comments, and good impact. So I wanted to thank them for that.

I'd like to say that our third quarter delivered 40% revenue growth and 36% gross margin, and a sharply narrowed adjusted EBITDA loss. We have that momentum, and we intend now to capitalize on it. We're seeing that we're creating brand awareness out there in Cycurion, and Cycurion is getting better known in both the US intelligence community, state and local government, and also on the corporate side. Our focus is going to continue on executing for clients and advancing predictive intelligence.

As an aside, I spent Thursday and Friday in a large cybersecurity event, the Cybersecurity Council, and I can tell you that there were quite a number of impressive CISOs there who actually reinforced our strategy of digital intelligence and being on the offense versus defense. At least three of the CISOs in their remarks stated that we've all been on defense too long. It's about time we move to offense. That truly validated the direction that we're going that Danny mentioned earlier, and we're excited about being ahead of the curve on that.

I want to thank all of our employees, by the way, for their continued hard work, our clients for their trust, and our shareholders for their continued interest in Cycurion. Thank you for joining us on this first earnings call today, and I hope you all have a great day.

Operator: This concludes Cycurion's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Thank you for participating, and you may now disconnect.

#3136. Need more AI in Creator Studio? Apple may charge you for it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With its new $50 AI usage packes, Apple is the latest company to introduce paid model for AI access.

There are plenty of AI subscriptions out there, but Apple’s AI features are among the few still accessible by simply purchasing a device. Now, Apple is shifting its business model by offering a one-time $50 purchase option to grant server-based AI capacity in some apps, starting with Creator Studio apps.

Apple is introducing a one-time purchase option for AI Usage Packs via app updates to Creator Studio. If you want expanded access to AI features in Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, the iWork Suite, and Logic Pro, you’ll need to pay.

Also: ChatGPT Plus vs. Google AI Pro: Two $20 plans, very different perks

The $50 fee applies to extra usage blocks and kicks in when you exceed predetermined limits in these apps. Instead of a recurring fee, Apple is hoping the one-time fee for intelligence usage packs will help the company offset some of the cost of AI. Users can buy a pack for Logic Pro now, and the other apps are expected to get it soon.

“Usage Packs may offer the option to prepay for the use of certain AI-based Services and represent the amount you have paid in advance for use of the respective Services,” according to Apple.

Apple’s one-time payment breaks away from what most companies are doing. Most companies offering AI tools try to offset the steep cost of running large language models (LLMs) by charging users for paid subscriptions. For example, Samsung is rumored to be planning such a subscription for Galaxy AI usage, including access to features that are currently free.

Also: The best tablets of 2026: Lab-tested recommendations

The Creator Studio apps are the only ones getting the Usage Packs for now. The legal terms for intelligence Usage Packs explain that these packs would be available in “AI apps,” which include not only Final Cut Pro, Compressor, Logic Pro, MainStage, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, but also Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Freeform, and other apps.

You’re not required to purchase the Usage Packs to enjoy the core functionality of the apps in the Creator Studio. However, the fact that the Usage Packs are to be applied to popular apps like Pages and Freeform begs the question of whether Apple plans to put a paywall on features that are currently free.

Some of the features for which you may be required to purchase Usage Packs once you exceed your limits include the generation of images, shapes, presentations, and presenter notes, as well as some assistant features. Usage limits reset each month.

Also: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Forget everything you knew about Amazon tablets

You can view your usage status for each of the applicable apps on your iPhone or iPad by tapping on More (or the button with three dots), then Intelligence Features, and Show Usage Status. On a Mac, it’s available by accessing Intelligence Features from the menu bar of the app you’re using, then clicking on Show Usage Status.

Intelligence usage packs expire after 12 months, but they roll over each month if left unused.

#3135. Razer’s Wild $1,000 Gaming Chair Has Six Motors, Built-In Speakers and RGB Lighting

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Gaming > Gaming Hardware > Gaming Accessories

The Soma Pro and Some Sense HD Haptics are part of an updated vibrating gaming chair lineup promising better immersion and improved comfort.

There are different levels of gaming immersion when it comes to haptics. On one side, you have controller haptics, which provide a bit of stimulation in games. You might feel a nice little rumble from explosions or gunshots and maybe a bit of vibration to give you some feedback while driving off-road.

On the other side, you have Razer’s two new gaming chairs, the $1,000 Soma Pro and the $570 Soma Sensa HD Haptics, which feature some serious motors to really shake your spine. Both incorporate Razer Sensa HD Haptics, which the company first debuted as part of Project Esther back in 2024. The chair also has THX Spatial Audio support and Razer Chroma RGB lighting built in.

This isn’t an entirely new line for Razer. The Soma series is one the company has been working on for some years now. The Soma Chroma was the first wireless RGB gaming chair announced this summer for $499. Now Razer is rounding out its gaming chair lineup.

“The Soma Pro is where the chair finally joins the game,” said Addie Tan, Razer’s global head of its lifestyle division in a press statement. “For years, gamers have upgraded everything they see and hear, while the seat they spend every session in stayed on the sidelines. With Soma Pro, the chair becomes part of the game — you feel it, hear it and see it.”

Both chairs come with six haptic motor actuators built into each seat, unlike the $300 Razer Freyja, which was essentially a wired cushion you placed on top of your existing chair and plugged in. I actually owned the Freyja, and while it worked OK for some games, for a lot of others I tried it with, it just used a generic rumble without really customizing things. It was also very uncomfortable to sit on long-term. Plus, I didn’t like the feeling of being tethered to a cable and ended up getting rid of it. A built-in wireless option, like these new chairs, seems like a much better solution to me.

Both new chairs deliver “multizone feedback” via Razer Sensa HD Haptics, and Razer says they should match the intensity, direction, and distance of in-game events. For example, an explosion off to the side will feel different from one that’s up close to you. So this isn’t just a generic rumble that applies to every situation; it’s customized based on the gameplay.

Razer lists more than 100 PC games that support integrated Sensa HD Haptics, including Battlefield 6, Borderlands 4, Marvel Rivals and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl. For everything else, the chairs use Audio-to-Haptics via Razer Synapse, converting audio into vibration, so the effect also works with games without native support, as well as with movies and music.

In theory, this should allow the feature to work on anything that supports controller vibration, but a Razer representative did not immediately respond to a request for clarification. On the Soma Pro, you can dial the overall intensity up or down in Synapse or adjust each of the six motor zones individually.

It’s worth noting that, unlike the Freyja, both chairs are wireless, though that doesn’t mean they’re completely untethered since Razer hasn’t managed to break the laws of energy yet. Each chair draws power over a single USB-C connection, from either a wall outlet or a compatible power bank, to preserve what Razer calls a wireless-aesthetic setup.

A power bank isn’t included in the box, so budget for one if you want the cable-free look. (You’ll also need a power adapter if you don’t have one handy, as the company doesn’t provide one.) That’s a downside because my LiberNovo Omni chair, which comes with adjustable lumbar support, a motorized spine, and even a massager setting, shipped with a rechargeable 2,200-mAh power bank.

Both Soma chairs carry a three-year warranty on mechanisms and moving parts and a two-year warranty on electronic parts.

Both Soma chairs share the same hardware, at least where you rest your backside. There’s a built-in lumbar arch intended to encourage a neutral sitting position, a dual-density cold-cured foam seat cushion with a softer top layer over a firmer core and a backrest that reclines up to 132 degrees. Both have a steel frame and are rated for people up to 331 pounds. Razer lists the Soma Pro for people 5 feet, 5 inches to 6 feet, 6 inches tall, and the Sensa model for people who are 5 feet, 3 inches to 6 feet, 6 inches.

For $1,000, the Soma Pro offers sound and light in addition to haptics. Built-in speakers deliver THX Spatial Audio directly from the chair. Yes, that’s right: You don’t need computer speakers — they’re right behind your head now. You can use them on their own or pair them with front speakers to widen the soundstage, with the chair effectively handling the rear of the setup. It is the same idea Razer has used with Razer Clio headrest speakers before, now integrated rather than clipped on.

Like the Soma Chroma, the Soma Pro has Razer Chroma RGB. The reactive lighting uses 16.8 million colors, responds to on-screen action in more than 300 integrated games and syncs with the rest of a Razer setup via Synapse. While I love a good light show, this isn’t really meant for the person seated in the chair. It seems designed for streamers and people watching you since it doesn’t look like you can really see the light show unless you take your eyes off the stream.

The Pro also gets the line’s most adjustable fit — 4D armrests, a magnetic head cushion and a frog tilt mechanism — on a powder-coated aluminum alloy wheelbase.

The controls are on a built-in panel that switches between Razer HyperSpeed Wireless (2.4 GHz) for PC and Bluetooth LE for mobile, with a companion Razer Furniture app on the Pro for adjusting haptics, audio and lighting from a phone. The controls are a nice alternative to using Razer’s annoyingly overlapping and often invasive Synapse and Chroma software.

The $570 Soma Sensa HD Haptics chair keeps the same six-actuator haptic system and drops the speakers and the RGB. That makes it $71 more than the lighting-only Soma Chroma ($499), and $430 less than the Soma Pro ($1,000). If you already have a headset or speakers, which I’d assume you do as a gamer who’s considering a product like this, the Soma Sensa HD Haptics gets you most of the key features without the unnecessary extras.

#3133. Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

With the November Patch Tuesday rollout, you can finally customize your right-click menu in Windows 11. But don't skip these security fixes.

Windows 11 users who’ve struggled to navigate and use the right-click menu in File Explorer now finally have some relief. With the November Patch Tuesday Windows update, you’re now able to customize the menu to add and remove specific commands and apps so that only your favorites appear.

As usual, the monthly update is mandatory, which means it should automatically download and install on your PC. To check, head to Settings and select Windows Update. If the latest update — labeled “2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974)” -– pops up as installed with a pending restart, just reboot your computer. Otherwise, click the button to check for updates and allow it to download and install.

Also: You can change Windows settings directly from a search now

One caveat: Microsoft’s monthly updates fully support Windows 11 26H2 and 25H2. But support for 24H2 ended last month, at least for the Home and Pro editions. Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education will continue to get monthly security updates, though not regular non-security preview updates, while Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise and Education will receive no more updates after this month.

If you use Windows 11 Home or Pro, be sure you upgrade your system to 26H2 to continue receiving the necessary support and updates.

First and foremost in the latest update is the new customizable right-click menu.

The context-sensitive right-click menu is a handy way to quickly access key settings, features, and apps, both in File Explorer and on the desktop. But there’s always been a flaw in its basic design. The more apps you install, the more cluttered and disorganized the menu becomes. That was especially problematic in previous versions of Windows. The old-style, classic menu would grow so long that it would be difficult to navigate and let you find the item you wanted.

With Windows 11, Microsoft introduced a more modern and pared-down menu. But this version can also get crowded. Plus, it may not display every command you need, so you often have to revert to the older classic menu. You’re then stuck dealing with two separate versions of the same menu, leading to an even more confusing and cumbersome experience.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says

The ideal solution is a menu that you can customize yourself, and that’s what we now have, at least that’s what is now rolling out. Microsoft calls this one a gradual rollout, which means you may or may not get it right away.

To see if and how this is available, open File Explorer and right-click on a folder or file. If the new menu has reached your PC, you’ll see an entry for Customize menu. Select that to view all the available options for tweaking it. Alternatively, head to Settings, select Personalization, and then click the entry for Context menu.

There, you’re able to turn certain file actions on or off, such as Send to, Print, Create shortcut, Copy as path, and Rotate image. You can also choose which apps appear all the time, either in the main menu or in a submenu. Plus, additional options let you decide where certain commands and actions appear and whether you can still access the old-style menu.

Though the customizable right-click menu is the star of the update, Microsoft has added other surprises as it strives to make Windows more reliable and user-friendly.

Also gradually rolling out, Cloud rebuild is a new recovery option that lets you reinstall Windows 11 via cloud-based system images and drivers downloaded from Windows Update. This tool can help you recover Windows when it won’t load and you don’t have a USB drive or your own custom image. The downside is that your files won’t survive. But if you regularly back them up as you should, you can restore them after Windows is back in business.

To start Cloud rebuild, go to Settings, select System, click Recovery, and then select Rebuild PC. Your PC will then restart into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to kick off the cloud rebuild. If Windows can load, your computer should automatically enter WinRE mode, where you can then choose the cloud rebuild. You should need to make sure your PC is online via a wired or wireless connection.

The November update also enhances or fixes other Windows features and apps.

And that then brings us to the security fixes.

This month’s update resolves 1,094 security vulnerabilities, according to Microsoft, with 63 of them rated critical and one already exploited in the wild. That’s fewer than October’s record of 1,400 patches. But it still represents a hefty number as Microsoft and other vendors continue to rely on AI to find and fix security holes.

Also: Windows finally gets a built-in internet speed test tool – how to try it

Though labeled Moderate, the exploited flaw points to a serious spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. Here, a remote attacker who sends you a malicious email and convinces you to open it could cause Outlook to connect to a network controlled by that attacker. In this case, though, you would not receive any warning. Further, the exploit might reveal your username and password to the sender, potentially allowing them to impersonate you.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it,” Jack Bicer, Director of Vulnerability Research at patch management provider Action1, said in an advisory.

“Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” Bicer explained further. “That quiet connection can leak the user’s NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs.”

#3130. Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you're an Ubuntu user considering a leap to Fedora, but you're hesitating, I explain why you should go ahead and just do it.

In the world of Linux, distro hopping is practically a spectator sport. At some point, we get bored with the distro we’re using and decide to try something new. Perhaps there’s a distro that offers better features, works with more hardware, or has a larger support community. There are so many reasons for switching distros.

Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: My verdict

However, for those new to Linux, the idea of leaving behind a distribution that’s been working just fine can be daunting, especially when you’re considering jumping to a distribution that isn’t as familiar and uses different technology.

As a new Linux user decades ago, I started with Caldera Open Linux 1.0 and immediately jumped to Red Hat Linux 5.2 (before Red Hat became Fedora). I stayed with Red Hat for years, until I found Ubuntu (I believe it was version 4).

Back then, making the jump wasn’t nearly as easy as it is now; in fact, it was unnerving. I was so used to how Fedora did things that I wasn’t certain I’d be able to acclimate.

But I did! And then, after realizing that hopping from one distro to another wasn’t the end of the world, I hopped around for a few years, from distro to distro until I settled back on Ubuntu-based distributions.

Also: Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next

It’s a lot, but it doesn’t have to be nearly as daunting as it seems. In fact, it can be exciting and fun. If you’re considering a jump from Ubuntu to Fedora, let me try to ease your concerns.

First, let’s get the obvious out of the way: Ubuntu and Fedora are both Linux. It’s not like you’re jumping from Windows or MacOS to Linux. This is a lateral move, which is not nearly as fear-inducing.

Beyond that, Ubuntu and Fedora are much more similar than you might expect. They both have GUI tools for everything you need; they’re both secure; they both have great package managers and package manager front-ends; they both make it easy to install all of the software you need (and all of the software you need is readily available); and they’re both user-friendly.

Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why

If you get beyond the GUI and dip your toes into the command line, they both (mostly) use the same commands. Yes, there are some variations, but when you’re first learning the CLI (if you ever do — it’s not necessary), you’ll find those basic commands on Ubuntu are exactly the same as they are on Fedora.

If you migrated from Windows to Ubuntu, you’ve already experienced what a faster operating system feels like. If you jump from Ubuntu to Fedora, you’re going to experience that again, because Fedora is (somewhat) faster than Ubuntu. The difference might not be as exaggerated as it was when you went from Windows to Linux, but it is noticeable. Animations are faster, apps open faster, and switching between desktops is faster — nearly every aspect of Fedora is a bit faster than in Ubuntu.

Also: Fedora 44 made me forget I was using Linux – in the best way

I’ve tested several aspects with regard to the speed of Ubuntu and Fedora, and here are my conclusions:

This is almost a tie. When rebooting from a logged-in desktop to the login screen, Fedora took 13.69 seconds, while Ubuntu took 14.31 seconds. The only caveat to that is if Fedora has updates that require a reboot, in which case Fedora takes considerably longer. The only time you have to reboot Ubuntu after an update is if the kernel is upgraded.

Fedora wins this one, especially when it comes to Flatpak and Snap apps. Snap apps simply cannot compete with the speed of Flatpak apps (more on this in a bit). I tested this by opening a Snap app on Ubuntu and a Flatpak app on Fedora, using GIMP (since I know GIMP takes a while to start). On Fedora, the Flatpak GIMP took 3.48 seconds, and on Ubuntu the Snap app version of GIMP took 4.34 seconds.

This is one area where Ubuntu has a slight edge, but only when installing via the default package manager (rather than Flatpak or Snap). I tested this by timing the installation of Audacity using each package manager (DNF5 and APT) from the command line. DNF5 installed Audacity in 15.34 seconds, whereas the Ubuntu installation took 14.61 seconds.

Generally speaking, Fedora not only ships with newer apps than Ubuntu, but it also gets updates faster than Ubuntu. That’s not to say that Ubuntu uses out-of-date packages; rather, Fedora is more cutting-edge than Ubuntu.

Also: 5 premium Linux distros absolutely worth paying for

At the same time, that doesn’t mean Fedora uses unstable applications. All software that ships and/or is updated on Fedora is well-tested and stable — it’s just fresher.

Flatpaks and Snaps are universal package managers. Fedora ships with Flatpak, and Ubuntu is all-in on Snaps. While these two technologies have the same goal (making software installation easier and more secure), they take different approaches.

First off, Flatpak was created by Red Hat, while Snap was created by Canonical. Snap is partially proprietary, while Flatpak is fully open-source. Flatpak enforces mandatory sandboxing, whereas Snap makes sandboxing optional. Flatpak apps launch faster than Snap apps. Finally, Snap packages are automatically updated, whereas Flatpak apps require manual updates.

Also: My favorite GNOME-based Linux distros

Overall, Flatpak is widely considered the superior technology by the Linux community.

In my experience, Flatpak is a better technology for the desktop, whereas Snap is best suited for servers.

If you were to look at both Ubuntu and Fedora, you would swear they use different desktop environments. Au contraire, mon ami. Both Fedora and Ubuntu use GNOME; the difference is that Ubuntu customizes GNOME to look more like the Ubuntu Unity UI Canonical tested back in 2010. Since then, Ubuntu adopted GNOME and customized it so it wouldn’t irk users who had grown accustomed to Unity.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

Fedora, on the other hand, sticks with a stock installation of GNOME for its flagship release. The good news is that, if you like the Ubuntu take on GNOME, you can install the necessary GNOME extensions (the main one being Dash to Panel) to get a similar layout. You can also get the Unity-like top bar by installing the Unite-Shell extension.

#3129. I Let My Apple Watch Eavesdrop on My Conversations for 2 Weeks

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

We’ve long suspected that our devices are listening to us, but what about when we invite them to do it? That’s what testing Audio Intelligence has felt like on the Apple Watch. But despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple says it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.

Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they said than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows)

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the important conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

#3128. Claude can collaborate in your team meetings soon – like an intern

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude is responding 'Yes' to that calendar invite - with some limitations. Plus: Anthropic launches two more new features that are available now.

Anthropic often refers to its Claude agent as your coworker. Soon, the company said, it will be able to join your meetings like one, and start working on the tasks you and your team are discussing live.

Also: I locked down my OpenClaw agent with Claude Code – then dared it to escape

“Claude Meetings will let you add Claude to a call to take notes and update the documents your team is working on during the conversation,” Anthropic said. The feature, which will be available for Team and Enterprise plans, theoretically goes beyond something like Gemini’s Google Meet transcription and note-taking, which identifies action items but doesn’t proactively contribute to them.

In material shared with ZDNET prior to the launch, the company said Claude “won’t join a call with outside guests unless an admin allows it, and it leaves if one joins anyway.” The company also said Claude Meetings will be on by default for Team plans, but Enterprise admins will be able to choose who gets it. The feature won’t work for organizations with “zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).”

The company did not clarify when Meetings would roll out, but announced several other updates for companies that are available now.

To further keep as much of your work ecosystem within the Claude universe, Anthropic released a new Whiteboards feature in beta.

Also: Claude’s Record-a-Skill cut my research to minutes

“Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time,” Anthropic said. Claude will group crowdsourced notes into themes and action items. Maybe double-check the results of that spew before locking anything in.

After brain-dumping like you might on a physical whiteboard, Anthropic said, Claude can turn that output into a deck or document, or export it to other tools for next steps.

A new Sheets feature is exactly as it sounds: Claude can now create shareable spreadsheets from a prompt and edit inside cells with trackable changes. But it’s not fully replacing the old guard of spreadsheets just yet.

“When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel,” Anthropic said. “You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.”

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free, local AI stack

Claude Dashboards, which only launched in beta last month, is now called Data. The tool can query company data from large external services such as Amazon Redshift and ClickHouse and comes with tracked changes and faster loading thanks to caching. According to Anthropic, it’s intended to let companies standardize metrics to avoid having conflicting data, surface data stories, and create a live source of truth everyone can access.

“With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access,” the company said.

Anthropic said that for Team plans, all three features are on by default. For Enterprise plans, only Claude Data will be on by default starting Nov. 19. Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, though you can adjust those settings in Artifacts.

Anthropic has maintained a lead over OpenAI by focusing on enterprise clients first, while OpenAI has prioritized several consumer products. Releases like this are unsurprising, as they serve Anthropic’s primary base. Both Anthropic and OpenAI are increasingly branching into workplace and productivity software for large-scale companies. That said, Anthropic’s recent release of a personal finance tool rivals OpenAI’s existing equivalent geared toward consumers.

Also: Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

In September, at its Dev Day, OpenAI released ChatGPT Space, which houses document and slide creation tools reminiscent of Google Workspace. Before that, Anthropic had similarly consolidated its document and slide creation features into a single hub.

If there’s a slight differentiator here versus Google Workspace, it’s interface seamlessness. Anthropic has designed Claude itself as the starting point for a range of workplace deliverables, rather than maintaining distinct applications that can quickly feel siloed.

#3127. Meet the Custom-Built Machine That Has Folded the iPhone Duo Nearly 500,000 Times

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Our Fold-a-Phone machine opens and closes Apple's iPhone Duo nearly a thousand times every hour.

We’re now nearly halfway through November, and CNET’s lab continues to work overtime testing Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this model of the Duo more than three weeks ago, and since then, its only job has been to bend and flatten.

How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? On Friday, Nov. 13, we passed 450,000 folds, and there was also an interesting change in the phone’s behavior.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

My team of engineers and testing experts has been watching the iPhone Duo open and close over and over for the past three weeks to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

#3126. Chase wass down for thousands — live updates on massive outage

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Chase bank appears to be suffering an online banking outage. On the outage tracking site, Down Detector, reports slowly starting rolling in this morning before suddenly spiking around 10 am Pacific.

Chase released a pair of statements throughout the nearly eight hour outage. The bank claimed that a technical issue brought its services down and was clear that it did not consider the issues a cyberattack.

Tom's Guide tried to confirm with the company but customers claimed that tellers at Chase locations couldn't operate their systems either. At least one support tweet on X seemed to confirm this.

Chase never said if its non-digital locations were compromised.

Here's what we learned throughout the day.

From what I can tell, the Chase outage finally appears to be over. Reports are still over 500 but most comments and social posts are indicating that people have access to their accounts again.

I have not a seen a "We're back" post from Chase or JPMorgan.

For awhile it seemed reports were in steady decline, but things have remained study for the last hour.

I am seeing mixed comments from people saying they have access, while others say they still can't login to the app.

Reports on Down Detector have halved in the last hour dropped from about 3,800 to 1,780.

Its been a slow decline but it appears things are coming back online for people.

People who've regained access have said they've been able to use Zelle, withdraw money and successfully login to the app or the browser.

I just received an update from Chase. Here's what the bank is saying now.

Per the bank's spokesperson, JPMorganChase apparently experienced a software bug in "on-premise hardware system", which the spokesperson reiterated there is "no evidence this is cyber-related."

The statement claims that customers still have access to their accounts and funds. They did not respond to questions about issues affecting brick-and-mortar banks.

"We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." It's unclear which timezone that end of day actually refers to.

Chase has been suffering a technical outage for more than 4 and a half hours.

Again, we saw an initial stream of reports around 7 am PT/10 am ET, with the real spike hitting two hours later.

Chase has said in statements that the problem is a technical one, not an attack. It's not clear what the issue is and it appears to affect both online banking and in-person transactions at their banks.

Reports have declined but not enough to declare the outage over. People are still reporting that they can't access their accounts.

We have asked Chase for clarification but haven't received any updates since the first statement.

After an initial decline, reports on Down Detector hit a momentary plateau. For the last half an hour, they've started a slow but steady decline.

Let me know if you're able to access your Chase account since reports started going down.

As of this writing, reports are under 3,200 for the first time since 10 am PT, about 3 hours ago.

Yahoo! Finance is tracking statements from different banks. Wells Fargo and Bank of America have received some outage reports, but not as many as Chase, which again suggests that it's an issue between Chase and other banks.

"You can still access your accounts through our ATMs, banking locations, and customer service," the Wells Fargo website reportedly reads.

I have a Wells Fargo account and could not find that statement, but I've also had no issues logging in or using my accounts online, so my experience may not be the same.

Bank of America has not released a statement.

A Chase spokesperson has responded to our inquiries with a similar statement as the one received by the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."

However, our statement had one extra line saying that the issue was not cyber-related, meaning it is something in the Chase systems and not a malicious attack.

"This is a technical issue, not cyber related.”

The spokesperson did not indicate how long it would take to resolve the issue or any potential causes.

Reports are starting to go Down Detector, though as of this posting they are still around 4,000 after a peak of 5,000 reports about 30 minutes ago.

Analyst Bruce Schneier (Security Technologist; Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School) is an internationally renowned security technologist.

We asked him why companies don't have redundancies to prevent outages:

"Redundancies reduce profitability, and it is the goal of shareholders these days to wring all excess profits out of any and every company. Thatreduces resilience in general, and redundancy in particular.”

With the Outlook outage last week, and more every day, Schneier expects more will come.

"I guess I’m not surprised. Our systems are very fragile these days. Fragile systems are the most profitable in the near term. And there is no incentive to focus on the long term.”

Chase has not responded to Tom's Guide as of this posting; however, a spokesperson did give a statement to the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete, but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson told the paper. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

This does seem to contradict users on social media claiming they can't log in.

I'm seeing reports and comments that people are having trouble logging into other banks including Bank of America and Wells Fargo.

I've been able to login into Wells, but that may not be universal.

Lets u know, are you having problems with your bank?

According to posters on Reddit, people have said that after attempting online transactions they ended up going to their location branch.

Multiple people said that the Chase tellers told them all their systems were down and they couldn't do anything.

"Then went to branch to ask about it they said they can’t do anything because their system is down smh," said one representative poster.

Tom's Guide has reached out to Chase for comment.

I am seeing hundreds of reports for Bank of America, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo and Zelle, but based on the amounts and the ability to log in to accounts with those banks, I currently believe this incident is isolated to Chase.

However, if you're trying to send or receive money from or to a Chase account, you will likely have problems.

Over on Down Detector reports started rolling in around 6:30 am Pacific/9:30 am ET but didn't really start spiking until 9:00 am PT. As of this posting there are more than 4,000 reports on the site.

@veeramarni We saw your post and want to reach out. I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience. ^RRNovember 16, 2026

So far, I haven't seen Chase say anything on any official channels as a formal post.

The best I've come across is from Chase Support on X where the company said that it is "working to resolve an issue with online banking."
