#3102. Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Google is moving digital keys out of individual smart lock apps and into the Google Wallet.

Google is adding digital home keys to Google Wallet, letting users tap their phones to unlock compatible smart locks. The home key functionality, which will integrate with Google Home, will roll out this month.

Also: This tiny box gives your older tech smart home superpowers

Apple introduced Home Keys in 2021 with iOS 15, allowing users to store digital keys in the Apple Wallet. This lets you tap your iPhone or Apple Watch on the lock to unlock it. More recently, the addition of Express Mode to Apple Home lets users unlock smart locks without first unlocking their iPhones with Face ID.

Google’s digital keys use tap-to-unlock via NFC on smart locks. Like the Apple Home Key, you don’t need to unlock your phone to use your digital key, though you can change your verification settings as you wish.

Google’s announcement confirms that the company is embracing Aliro and UWB unlocking technologies as well. UWB unlocking for smart locks is supported on Google Pixel 10 Pro and newer models, as well as select UWB-enabled Samsung Galaxy phones. Aliro is a common standard for compatible smart locks and devices.

Before Google’s announcement, compatible smart locks could be controlled on Android through their accompanying app and Google Home. Smart lock companies also offered their own digital access methods, like NFC cards, Bluetooth, and geolocation.

One digital key will be created for each Google Home, so it can unlock all compatible smart locks in that home. You won’t need to search through digital keys in Google Wallet to find the one for your front door, back door, or bedroom door — just tap your phone and Google Home will recognize the lock as one in your smart home ecosystem.

At launch, Google Wallet will support digital keys for the Aqara U400 with UWB and NFC, and NFC on the Schlage Sense Pro and Nuki Keypad 2.

Google Wallet already supports digital car keys for compatible vehicles.

#3099. Roku drops smart home products to focus on streaming – what that means for your devices

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Roku is winding down its smart home business following its sale to Fox. Here's what to know.

Roku is stepping back from smart home gear.

In an exclusive first reported by freelance journalist Janko Roettgers via his newsletter, Lowpass, the streaming device maker confirmed it won’t be making any additional smart home products going forward, as its existing home devices run out of stock.

“We’re sharpening our focus on Roku’s core mission: being the top streaming platform,” a Roku spokesperson told Roettgers via email. “As part of that, we plan to wind down sales of smart home hardware and will provide continued support and services for Roku Smart Home products.”

Also: Worried about Fox buying Roku? Here are three popular concerns – and why I’m optimistic

Roku was recently acquired by Fox, with the formal sale closing on Nov. 6.

Roku, primarily known for its streaming stick and TV devices that rival competitors like Amazon’s Fire lineup, expanded into the smart home space in 2022 with a series of affordable home security cameras, smart plugs, and lights, developed with white-labeled hardware from Waze. Roku launched its own product lineup with proprietary hardware in 2025.

Also: Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver – but you have alternatives

In 2024, the company launched TV features connected to its smart home products, including a view that let users cycle through their live camera feeds on their TV and a picture-in-picture feature that pins a feed to your screen while users have another app open. It’s unclear how this change will impact support for these cameras and associated features for those who already own them, but ZDNET has reached out to Roku for comment.

Roettgers said in his newsletter that, based on Roku’s own website, the number of products available for purchase appears to have dwindled. Currently, all but two of Roku’s smart home gear are listed as out of stock.

At other retailers like Home Depot, Amazon, and Walmart, many Roku listings have been removed or marked for clearance, while some retailers are only selling refurbished items.

It’s likely, as Roettgers identified in a previous newsletter, that Fox did not see long-term value in smart home gear for Roku, a fact certainly exacerbated by AI-induced hardware cost increases that have hit nearly every tech manufacturer, including Apple.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year – even legacy tech prices aren’t immune

The closure of the sale of Roku to Fox also emphasizes the return to streaming as the company’s main priority. Roettgers said the reason for that has been publicly noted in Roku’s financial disclosures, including last week’s 10-Q, where the brand clearly emphasized that smart home gear does not contribute to Roku’s streaming hours or revenue.

#3098. Grand Canyon Education: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Common App access brought over 5,600 applications in two months, a channel the company had never used before its ground growth push.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Grand Canyon Education (LOPE -1.07%) announced total enrollment increased 5.2% year over year. Long-term investors care because student retention and new campus formats drive scalable service revenue across education partners.

Three key takeaways from the call highlight where the business is headed.

Ground campus enrollment fell three percentage points below management expectations due to flat incoming student growth. Management launched four targeted programs to expand student reach and reignite campus growth over the next five years.

Grand Canyon University, the company's primary university partner, previously operated without access to the Common App, an online college application platform. Joining the platform generated over 5,600 applications during September and October, giving the institution direct access to high school applicants across the nation.

Off-campus hybrid locations deliver healthcare and nursing programs that generate more than three times the revenue per student compared to standard online programs. Growth in these specialized healthcare sites provides a higher-margin revenue stream as campus capacity expands across target regional markets.

Online enrollment growth remains steady as high student retention rates balance shifts in advertising spending and lower reentry counts.

The company relies on high program completion rates and expanding specialized degree offerings to maintain pricing power across its university partners. Management is watching site-level profit margins and capital allocation through share repurchases to compound long-term shareholder value.

#3097. I Put Xiaomi’s 18 Pro Max Camera to the Test and I Love the Results

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Xiaomi's bonkers dual-screen phone is here and I've been testing its camera.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi is taking the wraps off its phone in Paris tomorrow, but I’ve had the phone for the past few weeks and have been putting the camera to the test in my beautiful home of Edinburgh, Scotland, and in Paris, France. While it’s too early for me to share my full thoughts on the phone and its cameras (keep your eyes peeled tomorrow for that), I did want to share some of my favorite photos I’ve taken with the phone so far.

The images seen here are taken with the phone’s various built-in camera modes, largely the black and white mode, as I love the dramatic, filmic look it produces. They’re presented either as-shot or with minimal exposure adjustments using the phone’s built-in editing tools. Stay tuned for much more information on this phone and its wild second display on the back.

Taken using one of the phone’s built-in color styles, I love the vibrancy in this shot. The reds really pop, while the wider angle of the main camera emphasizes the tunnel effect of the alleyway, drawing the eye to the person and their dog.

I may be spoiling the rest of the images here by saying that this is my absolute favorite shot I’ve taken, but there we go. I took this using one of the dedicated black-and-white modes, and I think the tones here are perfect. Excellent dynamic range and contrast, and just the right amount of film grain. I positioned the figure between the buildings and had the phone almost on the floor to turn the rain-soaked tiles into a reflective surface to add some drama to this scene. I then applied a wide cinematic crop in post to give it that extra edge. Lovely stuff.

Most of my favorite photos with the phone were taken using the black-and-white mode. It’s no surprise; I shoot in black and white very often on my Leica Q3 43, and I used the monochrome mode for my favorite shots with Xiaomi’s Leitzphone earlier in the year.

The phone captures excellent black-and-white photos at night, too.

And by exposing for the bright highlights in this scene, I was able to create this stark, moody image of my handsome orange cat, Toulouse. Is he the best cat you’ve ever seen? Of course he is.

Back in color, this UFO that had presumably crash-landed in this Parisian market looks great in this filmic color mode. The oranges and reds pop against the other tones in this scene.

While this quick street portrait is similarly punchy.

I used manual mode here, taking full control over the white balance and exposure settings to achieve the tones I wanted. It’s a great-looking shot with excellent dynamic range. Xiaomi’s phone doesn’t appear to go too hard with its software processing either, meaning that even fine details look quite natural. Other Android phone-makers could take note.

As with the photo of Toulouse the cat, I exposed for the highlights here, forcing the rest of the scene under this bridge into shadow. As a result, it looks moody and dramatic but crucially it also looks exactly as I hoped it would. Many phones would try to artificially lift the shadows here, which would ruin the vibe I was going for.

I took this with the phone’s telephoto zoom lens, aiming to focus more on the digger as the subject and use the water for reflection. I love how this shot looks, especially in black and white, as the cloud detail behind it is especially noticeable.

While here I used the full wide angle of the main camera in order to create a lot of negative space around the figures, emphasizing the size of the building around them.

That building was Le Grande Arche in Paris and despite it being a miserably cold, wet and cloudy day I think the phone has captured a satisfyingly stark scene here.

I don’t like flying, so I distracted myself on the flight out to Paris by taking photos of things with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, including this man having a look out of the window.

And this shot of my plane’s wing somewhere above the UK. Again, in black and white. When it looks this good, why would I choose anything else?

And while we’re still in black and white, a particularly friendly pigeon. Hi, friend!

And to round us off, this dude in shades looking at a menu.

I’m genuinely really thrilled with so many of the shots I’ve taken with this phone. The black-and-white mode in particular is spectacular, and I’m looking forward to taking more shots with it. Stick around for more details on the phone — including the full review — coming soon.

I have this running bit where I call Robert Pattinson my girlfriend. It started sometime after "The Lighthouse" because old men gone bitter with yearning is very much my brand of terminally ill brain worm, and the joke's only gotten funnier with the stellar year the "Twilight" star's had. Yesterday, Amazon MGM Studios announced that Pattinson is taking up the mantle of 007, and I broke the news to the group chat with the following message: "my girlfriend is gonna be James Bond!" No explanation needed.

I've never seen a James Bond movie all the way through, a fact that shocked my (mostly male) coworkers this morning. Now that my favorite weird little guy is in the lead, I'm willing to break that streak. Before you go calling me a rabid fangirl, I have another confession: I first watched "Twilight" all the way through this year. I attempted once in high school but had to bail at the baseball scene where the level of unabashed white corniness on display had my eyes nearly rolling out of my skull.

No, my excitement for Pattinson's 007 reign doesn't stem from nostalgia, but from a quiet fascination that's sparked into an obsession over the past decade. This, the man who insists he's "spiritually Gen Z" despite pushing 40, who lies in interviews for fun, who dragged millions of screaming fans into theaters by being a brooding, sexy vampire for a series he openly despises. And I suspect his casting has activated those same millennial women like sleeper agents who will no doubt propel this latest Bond run into one of the most commercially successful to date. With many, like myself, turning out for their first Bond venture in theaters ever.

Action films are a notable blind spot in my cinema knowledge, one that I've been trying to fill in recent years since writing about streaming for Tom's Guide. It's not that I avoided them, per say, just that they didn't immediately appeal to me in the same way as my favorite genres — horror, art house, and damn near anything animated — did.

All the Jason Bournes, John Wicks, and Ethan Hunts of the world struck me as carbon copies of one another made in a lab to be propelled through one bombastic shoot out after the next. Now that I've caught up on a few of these iconic franchises, that opinion still rings true, though I've gained an appreciation for the kind of high-octane set pieces action fans still talk about to this day.

With Pattinson at the helm of the next Bond film, for the first time in my life, I'm excited to see a 007 movie in theaters. His talent and magnetism, even as some of the most pathetic characters I've ever seen on screen, is something straight out of the golden age of Hollywood.

Today's Bond announcement is the cherry on top of a year that's cemented Pattinson as a once in a generation acting talent. Between making our skin crawl as the charismatically slimy Chris Hansen in "Primetime" to going viral for shouting “somebody get these beggars out of here” in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster megahit “The Odyssey" and proving once again that no one does pathetic quite as well as he does in "The Drama," it's been a banner year for Pattison.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The British actor most known for his roles as Edward Cullen in “Twilight,” Cedric Diggory in "Harry Potter," and Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series will now succeed Daniel Craig as everyone's favorite suave superspy. There's no release date yet for Pattinson's debut as 007, though we do know Denis Villeneuve, who has already worked with Pattinson on the upcoming “Dune Part 3,” will be at the helm with a script by "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight.

It's clear Amazon MGM is trying to appeal to younger viewers with this pick too. After being around for over 70 years, James Bond's built a reputation as your father's (or maybe even grandfather's) favorite spy franchise. As Bruce Wayne in "The Batman," Pattinson proved he can bring a fresh edge to an iconic character without losing the mass appeal that makes a franchise work. With "The Batman" sequel currently in production, he’s also firmly established as a leading man audiences will turn out to see. For a franchise looking to usher in its next era, that's a pretty convincing résumé.

#3095. ‘We need more reviewers’: Finding Linux bugs is easy now – fixing them is another story

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some Linux maintainers are quitting under the crushing strain of AI bug reports, while others see signs for hope.

Recently, Microsoft’s FORGE Lab reported that its AI scanning system, MDASH, turned up 59 upstream Linux kernel bug reports, including one flaw at least 21 years old. That’s less impressive than it sounds. For 2026, through Nov. 2, the Linux Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) team reported an average of 27 CVEs a day.

Why so many? Easy: in Linux, any bug can be a security bug. As Linux Torvalds told me in 2024, “Bugs will happen, and anything can be a security bug if somebody is clever enough to just figure out how to abuse it.” Besides, since Linux runs everything from smartphones to refrigerators to supercomputers, what may be a serious bug in one device may not even appear at all on another.

It’s not just Linux, though. In the latest Windows Patch Tuesday security release, Microsoft reported 726 CVEs. The vast majority of these bug reports are coming from AI programmers. Finding bugs on anything is no longer the hard part. But reviewing and fixing them is, and both Microsoft developers and kernel maintainers are struggling to keep up.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

As the FORGE Lab said, “Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance.” Turning its findings into reports took more than four person-months because “human effort [is] the bottleneck.”

That’s hurting the overworked maintainers. On Nov. 10, an ARM engineer and Linux kernel maintainer Lorenzo Stoakes gave up reviewing code. He’d been a reviewer for the memory-management core, misc, reclaim, and Rust-related sections. Stoakes, a kernel contributor since 2014,  wrote, “Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain.”

Stoakes added, “Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I’d see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it’s pretty much half of what I see, if not more.”

Also: Filing bugs for open-source apps is a huge help for devs – and easier than you think

He’s not alone. As Greg Kroah-Hartman, the Linux kernel stable maintainer, said in a Q&A session at Open Source Summit Europe, “We don’t have enough people to review them, the onslaught of the LLM-generated patches. We need more reviewers. We don’t have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years.”

It’s not all doom and gloom, though. Linux Torvalds, Linux’s creator, said in a recent Linux Kernel Mailing List (LKML) message that much of the new code in the Linux 7.4 rc 2 “was driven by various AI fixes.”

He continued, “that on the bpf [Berkeley Packet Filter]- side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true. I think most other areas haven’t reached that point yet, but it’s at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn. Don’t hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we’ll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”

We can but hope. In an interview, Kroah-Hartman isn’t so optimistic. “We are getting closer, yes, but not quite there yet.”  He’s not even willing to give a guesstimate of when human-approved AI fixes will catch up with and overcome AI bug reports.

Also: I locked down my OpenClaw agent with Claude Code – then dared it to escape

Daniel Steinberg, the creator of the open-source cURL project, is also cautiously optimistic. Steinberg, who’s been especially critical of AI slop bug reports, told me in an interview that he now believes “we manage the flood pretty well so far, even if it goes a little up and down in periods depending exactly on who sends us a new set of findings this particular week.”

Still, while AI bugs remain a major headache for now, AI bug fixes, along with the work of thousands of maintainers, may finally be starting to stem the AI bug flood. I still foresee long days and nights of work ahead.

I also expect we’ll see more serious security breaches. In November alone, we saw a serious Linux TCP networking security hole revealed; the nasty Alpine Linux OpenSSH flaw; Alpine’s GitLab near-miss; and the wide-open PHP2Shell security problem, which many groups still haven’t patched.
